'''Telehealth''' is the use of electronic information and telecommunication technologies to support long-distance clinical health care, patient and professional health-related education, health administration, and public health. This includes data sharing by way of patient portals and electronic medical records. Telehealth encompasses a broad range of technologies and services used to provide patient care, health education, public health services, and health administration remotely using telecommunications technologies. <ref name="Shaw-2009">{{cite journal | vauthors = Shaw DK | title = Overview of telehealth and its application to cardiopulmonary physical therapy | journal = Cardiopulmonary Physical Therapy Journal | volume = 20 | issue = 2 | pages = 13–8 | date = June 2009 | pmid = 20467533 | pmc = 2845264 | doi = 10.1097/01823246-200920020-00003 }}</ref><ref name="CFP"/>

'''Telemedicine''' is sometimes used as a [[synonym]] but is actually a subset of telehealth. The Federation of State Medical Boards defines telemedicine as "the practice of medicine using electronic communication, information technology, or other means between a physician in one location, and a patient in another location, with or without an intervening health care provider." When rural settings, lack of transport, a lack of mobility, conditions due to outbreaks, epidemics or pandemics, decreased funding, or a lack of staff restrict access to care, telemedicine may bridge the gap<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mashima PA, Doarn CR | title = Overview of telehealth activities in speech-language pathology | journal = Telemedicine Journal and e-Health | volume = 14 | issue = 10 | pages = 1101–17 | date = December 2008 | pmid = 19119834 | doi = 10.1089/tmj.2008.0080 }}</ref> and can even improve retention in treatment<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lynch |first1=Joshua J. |last2=Payne |first2=Emily R. |last3=Varughese |first3=Renoj |last4=Kirk |first4=Hilary M. |last5=Kruger |first5=Daniel J. |last6=Clemency |first6=Brian |title=Comparison of 30-day retention in treatment among patients referred to opioid use disorder treatment from emergency department and telemedicine settings |journal=Journal of Substance Use and Addiction Treatment |date=October 2024 |volume=165 |article-number=209446 |doi=10.1016/j.josat.2024.209446 |pmid=38950782 }}</ref> as well as provide distance-learning; meetings, supervision, and presentations between practitioners; online information and [[health data]] management and healthcare system integration.<ref name="Miller-2007">{{cite journal | vauthors = Miller EA | title = Solving the disjuncture between research and practice: telehealth trends in the 21st century | journal = Health Policy | volume = 82 | issue = 2 | pages = 133–41 | date = July 2007 | pmid = 17046097 | doi = 10.1016/j.healthpol.2006.09.011 }}</ref> EHealth encompasses a wide range of applications, including but not limited to the following:<ref name="Office for the Advancement of Telehealth-2022">{{Cite web |last=<!-- no author attribution --> |date=March 2022 |title=What is TeleHealth? |url=https://www.hrsa.gov/telehealth/what-is-telehealth |access-date=12 January 2024 |website=Office for the Advancement of Telehealth |publisher=The Health Resources and Services Administration}}</ref><ref name="Shaw-2009" /><ref name="Miller-2007" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Barbosa |first1=William |last2=Zhou |first2=Kina |last3=Waddell |first3=Emma |last4=Myers |first4=Taylor |author5-link=Ray Dorsey |last5=Dorsey |first5=E. Ray |title=Improving Access to Care: Telemedicine Across Medical Domains |journal=[[Annual Review of Public Health]] |date=2021 |volume=42 |pages=463–481 |doi=10.1146/annurev-publhealth-090519-093711 |pmid=33798406 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

* Two [[clinician]]s discussing a case via [[Videoconferencing|video conference]]; 
* Robotic surgery performed through remote access; 
* Physical therapy conducted using digital monitoring instruments, live feed, and application combinations;
* Diagnostic tests transferred between facilities for interpretation by a higher specialist;
* Home monitoring through continuous transmission of patient health data;
* Online consultations between patients and practitioners;
* [[Video remote interpreting|Video remote interpretation]] services for clinical visits.

== Telehealth versus telemedicine ==
Telehealth is sometimes discussed interchangeably with telemedicine, the latter being more common than the former. Telehealth has been described as a disruptive innovation in healthcare because it enables medical services to be delivered remotely using communication technologies. The [[Health Resources and Services Administration]] distinguishes telehealth from telemedicine in its scope, defining telemedicine only as describing remote clinical services, such as diagnosis and monitoring, while telehealth includes [[Preventive healthcare|preventative]], promotive, and curative care delivery.<ref name="Office for the Advancement of Telehealth-2022" /> This includes the above-mentioned non-clinical applications, like administration and provider education.<ref name="Shaw-2009" /><ref name="CFP"/>

The [[United States Department of Health and Human Services]] states that the term telehealth includes "non-clinical services, such as provider training, administrative meetings, and continuing medical education", and that the term telemedicine means "remote clinical services".<ref name="Tss5ihId">{{cite web |url=http://americasmarkets.usatoday.com/2015/07/01/teladoc-shares-surge-more-than-50-in-healthy-ipo-debut/ |title=Teladoc shares surge 50% in healthy IPO debut |access-date=2015-07-02 |date=2015-07-01 |work=[[USA Today]] | vauthors = Mitchell B }}</ref>
The [[World Health Organization]] uses telemedicine to describe all aspects of health care including preventive care.<ref name="who">{{cite book |title=Telemedicine: opportunities and developments in Member States: report on the second global survey on eHealth |date=2010 |publisher=World Health Organization |isbn=978-92-4-156414-4 |hdl=10665/44497 |hdl-access=free }}{{pn|date=July 2025}}</ref> The [[American Telemedicine Association]] uses the terms telemedicine and telehealth interchangeably, although it acknowledges that telehealth is sometimes used more broadly for remote health not involving active clinical treatments.<ref name="ATA">{{cite web|url=http://www.americantelemed.org/learn/what-is-telemedicine|title=What is Telemedicine?|publisher=American Telemedicine Association|location=Washington, D.C.|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130508215350/http://www.americantelemed.org/learn/what-is-telemedicine|archive-date=8 May 2013|access-date=21 August 2011}}</ref>

[[eHealth]] is another related term, used particularly in the U.K. and Europe, as an umbrella term that includes telehealth, [[electronic medical record]]s, and other components of [[health information technology]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Della Mea |first1=Vincenzo |title=What is e-Health (2): The death of telemedicine? |journal=Journal of Medical Internet Research |date=22 June 2001 |volume=3 |issue=2 |article-number=e22 |doi=10.2196/jmir.3.2.e22 |doi-access=free |pmid=11720964 |pmc=1761900 }}</ref>

== Methods and modalities ==
{{Further|List of video telecommunication services and product brands}}
Telehealth requires good Internet access by participants, usually in the form of a strong, reliable [[broadband]] connection, and broadband mobile communication technology of at least the fourth generation (4G) or long-term evolution (LTE) standard to overcome issues with video stability and bandwidth restrictions.<ref name="pmid32224764">{{cite journal | vauthors = Alexandrov AW, Alexandrov AV | title = Innovations in Prehospital Stroke Management Utilizing Mobile Stroke Units | journal = Continuum | location = Minneapolis, Minn. | volume = 26 | issue = 2 | pages = 506–512 | date = April 2020 | pmid = 32224764 | doi = 10.1212/CON.0000000000000850 }}</ref><ref name="pmid26641366">{{cite journal | vauthors = Itrat A, Taqui A, Cerejo R, Briggs F, Cho SM, Organek N, Reimer AP, Winners S, Rasmussen P, Hussain MS, Uchino K | title = Telemedicine in Prehospital Stroke Evaluation and Thrombolysis: Taking Stroke Treatment to the Doorstep | journal = JAMA Neurology | volume = 73 | issue = 2 | pages = 162–8 | date = February 2016 | pmid = 26641366 | doi = 10.1001/jamaneurol.2015.3849 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="pmid28872449">{{cite journal | vauthors = Audebert H, Fassbender K, Hussain MS, Ebinger M, Turc G, Uchino K, Davis S, Alexandrov A, Grotta J | collaboration = PRESTO Group | title = The PRE-hospital Stroke Treatment Organization | journal = International Journal of Stroke| volume = 12 | issue = 9 | pages = 932–940 | date = December 2017 | pmid = 28872449 | doi = 10.1177/1747493017729268 | doi-access = free }}</ref> As broadband infrastructure has improved, telehealth usage has become more widely feasible.<ref name="Office for the Advancement of Telehealth-2022" /><ref name="Shaw-2009" />

[[Health professional|Healthcare providers]] often begin telehealth with a [[needs assessment]] which assesses hardships that can be improved by telehealth such as travel time, costs or time off work.<ref name="Office for the Advancement of Telehealth-2022" /><ref name="Shaw-2009" /> Collaborators such as [[Technology company|technology companies]] can ease the transition.<ref name="Office for the Advancement of Telehealth-2022" />

Delivery can come within four distinct domains: [[Live video streaming|live video (synchronous)]], [[Store and forward|store-and-forward (asynchronous)]], [[remote patient monitoring]], and [[MHealth|mobile health]].<ref name="The Center for Connected Health Policy" /> Audio-based telemedicine, primarily through telephone consultations, has been studied as a tool for managing chronic conditions. A systematic review of 40 randomized controlled trials found that audio-based care was generally comparable to in-person or video care, though with low to very low certainty of evidence.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Albritton |first1=Jordan A. |last2=Booth |first2=Graham |last3=Kugley |first3=Shannon |last4=Reddy |first4=Shivani |last5=Coker-Schwimmer |first5=Manny |last6=Fujita |first6=Miku |last7=Crotty |first7=Karen |date=2025 |title=Audio-Based Care for Managing Chronic Conditions in Adults: A Systematic Review |journal=Medical Care |volume=63 |issue=2 |pages=164–182 |doi=10.1097/MLR.0000000000002097 |pmc=11708983 |pmid=39791849}}</ref>

=== Store and forward ===
[[Store and forward|Store-and-forward]] telemedicine (also known as asynchronous telehealth<ref>{{cite web |url=https://telehealth.hhs.gov/providers/best-practice-guides/direct-to-consumer/asynchronous-direct-to-consumer-telehealth |website=US Department of Health & Human Services |publisher=hhs.gov |access-date=24 September 2024}}</ref>) involves acquiring medical data (like [[Medical imaging|medical images]], [[biosignal]]s etc.) and then transmitting this data to a doctor or medical specialist at a convenient time for assessment [[offline]].<ref name="ATA"/> It does not require the presence of both parties at the same time.<ref name="Sachpazidis">{{cite thesis|url=https://www.consultingradiologists.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/Dissertation-final-10Nov2008.pdf|title=Image and Medical Data Communication Protocols for Telemedicine and Teleradiology (dissertation)|publisher=Department of Computer Science, Technical University of Darmstadt|location=Darmstadt, Germany|date=10 Jul 2008 | vauthors = Sachpazidis I |access-date=14 Aug 2018}}</ref> [[Dermatology]] (cf: [[teledermatology]]), [[radiology]], and [[pathology]] are common specialties that are conducive to asynchronous telemedicine. A properly structured [[medical record]], preferably in [[Electronic medical record|electronic]] form, should be a component of this transfer. The 'store-and-forward' process requires the clinician to rely on a history report and audio/video information in lieu of a physical examination.<ref name="ATA"/>

=== Remote monitoring ===
[[File:Beurer BM26 sphygmomanometer.jpg|thumb|A blood pressure monitor]]
[[Remote patient monitoring|Remote monitoring]], also known as self-monitoring or testing, enables medical professionals to monitor a patient remotely using various technological devices. This method is primarily used for managing chronic diseases or specific conditions, such as heart disease, diabetes mellitus, or asthma. These services can provide comparable health outcomes to traditional in-person patient encounters, supply greater satisfaction to patients, and may be cost-effective.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Salehahmadi Z, Hajialiasghari F | title = Telemedicine in iran: chances and challenges | journal = World Journal of Plastic Surgery | volume = 2 | issue = 1 | pages = 18–25 | date = January 2013 | pmid = 25489500 | pmc = 4238336 }}</ref> Examples include home-based nocturnal [[Kidney dialysis|dialysis]],<ref name="pmid10569098">{{cite journal | vauthors = Pierratos A | title = Nocturnal hemodialysis: dialysis for the new millennium | journal = Canadian Medical Association Journal | volume = 161 | issue = 9 | page = 1137 | date = November 1999 | pmid = 10569098 | pmc = 1230743 }}</ref> improved joint management,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Koutras C, Bitsaki M, Koutras G, Nikolaou C, Heep H | title = Socioeconomic impact of e-Health services in major joint replacement: A scoping review | journal = Technology and Health Care | volume = 23 | issue = 6 | pages = 809–17 | date = 17 August 2015 | pmid = 26409523 | doi = 10.3233/THC-151036 }}</ref> and diabetes care using audio-based telemedicine with remote monitoring tools.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Reddy |first1=Shivani |last2=Booth |first2=Graham |last3=Coker-Schwimmer |first3=Manny |last4=Kugley |first4=Shannon |last5=Rodriguez-Borja |first5=Ivette |last6=Patel |first6=Sheila V. |last7=Fujita |first7=Miku |last8=Philbrick |first8=Sarah |last9=Ruwala |first9=Richa |last10=Albritton |first10=Jordan A. |last11=Crotty |first11=Karen |title=Audio-Based Care for Managing Diabetes in Adults: A Systematic Review |journal=Medical Care |date=February 2025 |volume=63 |issue=2 |pages=152–163 |doi=10.1097/MLR.0000000000002096 |pmc=11708993 |pmid=39791848 }}</ref>

=== Real-time interactive ===
[[Electronic consultation]]s are possible through interactive telemedicine services which provide real-time interactions between patient and provider.<ref name="Sachpazidis" /> [[Videotelephony|Videoconferencing]] has been used in a wide range of clinical disciplines and settings for various purposes, including management, diagnosis, counseling, and monitoring of patients.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Fatehi F, Armfield NR, Dimitrijevic M, Gray LC | title = Clinical applications of videoconferencing: a scoping review of the literature for the period 2002-2012 | journal = Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare | volume = 20 | issue = 7 | pages = 377–83 | date = October 2014 | pmid = 25399998 | doi = 10.1177/1357633X14552385 }}</ref>

=== Videotelephony ===
{{main|Videotelephony}}

Videotelephony comprises the technologies for the reception and transmission of audio-video signals by users at different locations for communication between people in real time.<ref name=McGrawHill>McGraw-Hill Concise Encyclopedia of Engineering. [http://encyclopedia2.thefreedictionary.com/Videotelephony Videotelephony], McGraw-Hill, 2002. Retrieved from the FreeDictionary.com website, January 9, 2010</ref>

At the dawn of the technology, videotelephony also included ''image phones'' which would exchange still images between units every few seconds over conventional [[Plain old telephone service|POTS]]-type telephone lines, essentially the same as [[Slow-scan television|slow scan TV]] systems.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rodriguez |first=Ernesto J. |chapter=Computer support for an experimental PICTUREPHONE®/Computer system at Bell Telephone Laboratories, Incorporated |date=1971 |title=Proceedings of the May 16-18, 1972, spring joint computer conference on - AFIPS '72 (Spring) |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1145/1479064.1479078 |location=New York, New York, USA |publisher=ACM Press |pages=71 |doi=10.1145/1479064.1479078}}</ref>

Currently, videotelephony is particularly useful to the [[deaf]] and [[Speech disorder|speech-impaired]] who can use it with [[sign language]] and also with a [[Video Relay Service|video relay service]], as well as to those with [[disability|mobility issues]] or those who are located in distant places and are in need of [[telerehabilitation|telemedical]] or [[distance education|tele-educational]] services.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-07-18 |title=Video Relay Services {{!}} Federal Communications Commission |url=https://www.fcc.gov/consumers/guides/video-relay-services?utm_source=chatgpt.com |access-date=2025-04-18 |website=www.fcc.gov |language=en}}</ref>{{AI-retrieved source|date=March 2026|checked=no}}<ref>{{Cite web |title=NAD - National Association of the Deaf |url=https://www.nad.org/resources/technology/telephone-and-relay-services/video-relay-services/ |access-date=2025-04-18 |website=www.nad.org}}</ref>

==Categories==
=== Emergency care ===
[[File:US Navy 060518-N-2832L-013 Senior training specialist with Multi-Services Group International (MSGI), Michael Bedwell, trains Sailors to use Battlefield Medical Information Systems Telemedicine (BMIST) equipped Personal Digital.jpg|thumb|U.S. Navy medical staff being trained in the use of handheld telemedical devices (2006)]]
Common daily emergency telemedicine is performed by SAMU Regulator Physicians in [[France]], [[Spain]], [[Chile]], and [[Brazil]]. [[Aircraft]] and [[Maritime transport|maritime]] emergencies are also handled by SAMU centres in Paris, Lisbon and Toulouse.<ref>George R. Schwartz, C. Gene Cayten; George R. Schwartz (editor). [https://books.google.com/books?id=NlZ_aST4_hcC Principles and Practice of Emergency Medicine, Volume 2], Lea & Febiger, 1992, pg.3202, {{ISBN|0-8121-1373-X}}, {{ISBN|978-0-8121-1373-0}}.</ref>

A recent study identified three major barriers to the adoption of telemedicine in emergency and critical care units. They include:
* Regulatory challenges related to the difficulty and cost of obtaining licensure across multiple states, malpractice protection and privileges at multiple facilities
* Financial barriers including a lack of acceptance and reimbursement by government payers and some commercial insurance carriers, which places the investment burden squarely upon the hospital or healthcare system.
* Cultural barriers occurring from the lack of desire, or unwillingness, of some physicians to adapt clinical paradigms for telemedicine applications.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Rogove HJ, McArthur D, Demaerschalk BM, Vespa PM | title = Barriers to telemedicine: survey of current users in acute care units | journal = Telemedicine Journal and e-Health | volume = 18 | issue = 1 | pages = 48–53 | date = January–February 2012 | pmid = 22082107 | doi = 10.1089/tmj.2011.0071 }}</ref>
[[File:Операционная. ФЦН (Тюмень) 01.JPG|thumb|Telemedicine system. ''[[Federal Center of Neurosurgery (Tyumen)|Federal Center of Neurosurgery in Tyumen]]'' (2013)]]

Emergency telehealth is also gaining acceptance in the [[United States]]. There are several modalities currently being practiced that include but are not limited to TeleTriage, TeleMSE, and ePPE.

An example of telehealth in the field is when [[Emergency medical services|Emergency Medical Services]] (EMS) arrive on the scene of an incident and are able to perform an [[Electrocardiography|electrocardiogram]] (EKG) that is then sent directly to a physician at the hospital to be read, allowing for prompt care and management..<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Langabeer JR, Champagne-Langabeer T, Alqusairi D, Kim J, Jackson A, Persse D, Gonzalez M | title = Cost-benefit analysis of telehealth in pre-hospital care | journal = Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare | volume = 23 | issue = 8 | pages = 747–751 | date = September 2017 | pmid = 27913657 | doi = 10.1177/1357633X16680541 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

=== Telenursing ===
{{main|Telenursing}}

[[File:Telehealth Teleiechyd - Welsh Government video; 2016.webm|thumb|A short video on telenursing by the [[Welsh Government]] (2016)]]
Telenursing refers to the use of [[telecommunications]] and [[information technology]] in order to provide [[nursing]] services in health care whenever a large physical distance exists between patient and nurse, or between any number of nurses. As a field, it is part of telehealth, and has many points of contact with other medical and non-medical applications, such as [[telediagnosis]], teleconsultation, telemonitoring, etc.

Telenursing is achieving significant growth rates in many countries due to several factors: the preoccupation with reducing the costs of health care, an increase in the [[aging]] and chronically ill population, and the increase in coverage of health care to distant, rural, small or sparsely populated regions. Among its benefits, telenursing may help solve increasing shortages of nurses, reduce distances and travel time, and keep patients out of hospital. A greater degree of job satisfaction has been registered among telenurses.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.e-health-insider.com/news/item.cfm?ID=1263 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060618103208/http://www.e-health-insider.com/news/item.cfm?ID=1263 | archive-date = 18 June 2006 | title = Nurses Happier Using Telecare, Says International Survey | publisher = eHealth Insider | date = 15 June 2005 | access-date = 4 April 2009 }}</ref>

In [[Australia]], during January 2014, [[Melbourne]] tech startup [[Small World Social]] collaborated with the [[Australian Breastfeeding Association]] to create the first hands-free breastfeeding [[Google Glass]] application for new mothers.<ref name="Lactation Help">{{cite web|title=Google Glass connects breastfeeding moms with lactation help|url=http://www.inquisitr.com/1224638/google-glass-connects-breastfeeding-moms-with-lactation-help/|website=Inquisitr|date=24 April 2014 |access-date=12 June 2014}}</ref> The application, named [[Google Glass Breastfeeding app trial]], allows mothers to nurse their baby while viewing instructions about common breastfeeding issues (latching on, posture, etc.) or call a lactation consultant via a secure Google Hangout,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://vimeo.com/87625169|title=Breastfeeding Walkthrough for Mothers and Counselors|first=Small World|last=Social|date=25 February 2014|via=Vimeo}}</ref> who can view the issue through the mother's Google Glass camera.<ref name="Jumpin Today Show">{{cite web|title=Exclusive Clips Google glasses help breastfeeding mums|url=http://www.jump-in.com.au/show/today/videos/3496995149001/|website=Jumpin Today Show|publisher=Mi9 Pty. Ltd.|access-date=12 June 2014|archive-date=11 July 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140711191133/http://www.jump-in.com.au/show/today/videos/3496995149001/}}</ref> The trial was successfully concluded in [[Melbourne]] in April 2014, and 100% of participants were breastfeeding confidently.<ref>{{cite news| url=http://www.smh.com.au/technology/technology-news/breastfeeding-mothers-get-help-from-google-glass-and-small-world-20140118-311s3.html | work=The Sydney Morning Herald | title=Breastfeeding mothers get help from Google Glass and Small World}}</ref><ref name="Google Glass">{{cite web|title=Turns Out Google Glass Is Good for Breastfeeding|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/turns-out-google-glass-is-good-for-breastfeeding/|publisher=Motherboard Vice Media Inc.|access-date=1 May 2014|date=21 April 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.smallworldsocial.com/|title=SWS Website - We transfer complex and tacit knowledge|website=SWS Website}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://breastfeeding.smallworldsocial.com/|title=Breastfeeding Support Project - Small World Social|date=23 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140423100600/http://breastfeeding.smallworldsocial.com/|archive-date=2014-04-23}}</ref>

=== Telepalliative care ===
[[Palliative care]] is an [[Interdisciplinarity|interdisciplinary]] medical [[Caregiver|caregiving]] approach aimed at optimizing [[quality of life]] and mitigating [[suffering]] among people with serious, complex, and often [[Terminal illness|terminal]] [[Disease|illnesses]]. In the past, palliative care was a [[disease]] specific approach, but today the [[World Health Organization]] (WHO) takes a broader approach suggesting that palliative care should be applied as early as possible to any chronic and fatal illness. Challenging aspects of the use of telehealth in palliative care have also been described. Generally, palliative care is a diverse [[Medicine|medical]] specialty, involving [[Interdisciplinarity|interdisciplinary]] [[professional]]s from different professional [[tradition]]s and [[culture]]s, delivering care to a [[Homogeneity and heterogeneity|heterogenous]] [[Cohort (statistics)|cohort]] of patients with diverse diseases, conditions and symptoms. This makes it a challenge to develop telehealth that is suitable for all patients and in all contexts of palliative care. Some of the barriers to telepalliative care relate to inflexible reporting of complex and fluctuating symptoms and circumstances using electronic questionnaires.<ref name="Steindal-2023" /> Further, palliative care emphasizes a [[Holism|holistic]] approach that should address [[Existentialism|existential]], spiritual and [[Mental health|mental]] distress related to serious illness.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What Are Palliative Care and Hospice Care? |url=https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/what-are-palliative-care-and-hospice-care |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171004193041/https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/what-are-palliative-care-and-hospice-care |archive-date=October 4, 2017 |access-date=2023-04-27 |website=National Institute on Aging |date=14 May 2021 |language=en}}</ref> However, few studies have included the self-reporting of existential or spiritual concerns, [[emotion]]s, and [[well-being]].<ref name="Steindal-2023" /> Healthcare professionals may also be [[Comfort|uncomfortable]] providing emotional or [[Psychology|psychological]] care remotely.<ref name="Lundereng-2023" /> Palliative care has been characterized as high-touch rather than high-tech, limiting the interest in applying technological advancements when developing interventions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Head |first1=Barbara A. |last2=Schapmire |first2=Tara J. |last3=Zheng |first3=Yongqiang |title=Telehealth in Palliative Care: A Systematic Review of Patient-Reported Outcomes |journal=Journal of Hospice & Palliative Nursing |date=April 2017 |volume=19 |issue=2 |pages=130–139 |doi=10.1097/NJH.0000000000000319 }}</ref> To optimize the advantages and minimize the challenges with the use of telehealth in [[Home care|home-based]] palliative care, [[future]] [[research]] should include users in the [[design]] and development [[process]]. Understanding the potential of telehealth to support [[Therapy|therapeutic]] relationships between patients and health care professionals and being aware of the possible difficulties and tensions it may create are critical to its [[success]]ful and [[Acceptability|acceptable]] use.<ref name="Lundereng-2023" /><ref name="Steindal-2023" />

=== Telepharmacy ===
[[File:Winn Army Community Hospital Pharmacy Stays Online During Power Outage.jpg|thumb|alt=Pharmacists filling prescriptions at a computer | Pharmacy personnel deliver [[medical prescription]]s electronically. Remote delivery of [[pharmaceutical care]] is an example of telemedicine.]]
{{main|Telepharmacy}}

Telepharmacy is the delivery of [[pharmaceutical care]] via [[telecommunications]] to patients in locations where they may not have direct contact with a [[pharmacist]]. It is an instance of the wider phenomenon of telemedicine, as implemented in the field of [[pharmacy]]. Telepharmacy services include [[drug therapy]] monitoring, patient counseling, prior authorization and refill authorization for [[prescription drugs]], and monitoring of [[Formulary (pharmacy)|formulary]] compliance with the aid of [[teleconferencing]] or [[videoconferencing]]. [[Remote dispensing]] of medications by automated packaging and labeling systems can also be thought of as an instance of telepharmacy. Telepharmacy services can be delivered at retail pharmacy sites or through [[Hospital|hospitals]], [[Nursing home|nursing homes]], or other medical care facilities. This approach allows patients in remote or underserved areas to receive pharmacy services that would otherwise be unavailable to them, enhancing access to care and ensuring continuity in medication management.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Poudel |first1=Arjun |last2=Nissen |first2=Lisa M. |date=2016-10-26 |title=Telepharmacy: a pharmacist's perspective on the clinical benefits and challenges |journal=Integrated Pharmacy Research and Practice |language=English |volume=5 |pages=75–82 |doi=10.2147/IPRP.S101685 |doi-access=free |pmc=5741040 |pmid=29354542}}</ref> Health outcomes appear similar when pharmacy services are delivered by telepharmacy compared to traditional service delivery.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lowry SJ, Kay CN, Marsom EN, Park JS, Poole S, Page AT | title=Optimising health outcomes via pharmacist delivered telehealth medicines management: a systematic review | journal=Journal of Pharmacy Practice and Research | publisher=Wiley | volume=50 | issue=5 | year=2020 |doi=10.1002/jppr.1695 | pages=377–390 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

The term can also refer to the use of videoconferencing in pharmacy for other purposes, such as providing education, training, and management services to pharmacists and pharmacy staff remotely.<ref name="Angaran" />

=== Telenutrition ===
Telenutrition refers to the use of video conferencing/ telephony to provide online consultation by a [[nutritionist]] or [[Dietitian|dietician]]. Patient or clients upload their vital statistics, diet logs, food pictures, etc., on a telenutrition portal that is then used by the nutritionist or dietician to analyze their current health condition. The nutritionist or dietician can then set goals for their respective clients/patients and monitor their progress regularly by follow-up consultations.

Telenutrition portals can help people seek remote consultation for themselves and/or their family. This can be extremely helpful for elderly or bedridden patients who can consult their dietician from comfort of their homes.

Telenutrition showed to be feasible, and the majority of patients trusted the nutritional televisits, in place of the scheduled but not provided follow-up visits during the lockdown of the COVID-19 pandemic.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Costantino |first1=Andrea |last2=Roncoroni |first2=Leda |last3=Noviello |first3=Daniele |last4=Nandi |first4=Nicoletta |last5=Lombardo |first5=Vincenza |last6=Scricciolo |first6=Alice |last7=Scaramella |first7=Lucia |last8=Vecchi |first8=Maurizio |last9=Elli |first9=Luca |title=Nutritional and Gastroenterological Monitoring of Patients With Celiac Disease During COVID-19 Pandemic: The Emerging Role of Telemedicine and Point-of-Care Gluten Detection Tests |journal=Frontiers in Nutrition |date=13 April 2021 |volume=8 |article-number=622514 |doi=10.3389/fnut.2021.622514 |doi-access=free |pmid=33928109 |pmc=8076748 }}</ref>

=== Telerehabilitation ===
{{main|Telerehabilitation}}

[[File:Telemedicine in rehabilitation 2.jpg|thumb|Telemedicine in rehabilitation]]
Telerehabilitation (or ''e-rehabilitation''<ref name="dl-2005">{{cite book |editor1-last=Tan |editor1-first=Joseph |title=E-Health Care Information Systems: An Introduction for Students and Professionals |date=2005 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-0-7879-7741-2 |page=219 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Keaton |first1=Lisa |last2=Pierce |first2=Linda |last3=Steiner |first3=Victoria |last4=Lance |first4=Karen |last5=Masterson |first5=Michelle |last6=Rice |first6=Martin |last7=Smith |first7=Julie |title=An E-rehabilitation Team Helps Caregivers Deal with Stroke |journal=Internet Journal of Allied Health Sciences and Practice |date=2004 |doi=10.46743/1540-580X/2004.1057 }}</ref>) is the delivery of [[Physical medicine and rehabilitation|rehabilitation]] services over [[telecommunication network]]s and the Internet. Most types of services fall into two categories: clinical assessment (the patient's functional abilities in his or her environment) and [[medical therapy|clinical therapy]]. Some fields of rehabilitation practice that have explored telerehabilitation are: [[neuropsychology]], [[speech–language pathology]], [[audiology]], [[occupational therapy]], and [[physical therapy]]. Telerehabilitation can deliver therapy to people who cannot travel to a [[clinic]] because the patient has a [[disability]] or because of travel time. Telerehabilitation also allows experts in rehabilitation to engage in clinical consultation at a distance.

Most telerehabilitation is highly visual. As of 2014, the most commonly used mediums are [[webcam]]s, [[videoconferencing]], [[phone line]]s, [[videophone]]s, and webpages containing [[Rich Internet Application|rich web applications]]. The visual nature of telerehabilitation technology limits the types of rehabilitation services that can be provided. It is most widely used for [[neuropsychological rehabilitation]], fitting of rehabilitation equipment such as [[wheelchair]]s, [[Brace (orthopaedic)|braces]], or [[artificial limb]]s, and in speech-language pathology. [[Rich web applications]] for neuropsychological rehabilitation ([[cognitive rehabilitation]]) of cognitive impairment (from many etiologies) were first introduced in 2001. This endeavor has expanded as a [[teletherapy]] application for cognitive skills enhancement programs for school children. [[Tele-audiology]] (hearing assessments) is a growing application. Physical therapy and psychology interventions delivered via telehealth may result in similar outcomes as those delivered in person for a range of health conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Raymond |first1=Melissa J. |last2=Christie |first2=Lauren J. |last3=Kramer |first3=Sharon |last4=Malaguti |first4=Carla |last5=Mok |first5=Zaneta |last6=Gardner |first6=Betina |last7=Giummarra |first7=Melita J. |last8=Alves-Stein |first8=Serena |last9=Hudson |first9=Claire |last10=Featherston |first10=Jill |last11=Holland |first11=Anne E. |last12=Lannin |first12=Natasha A. |date=2024-02-07 |title=Delivery of Allied Health Interventions Using Telehealth Modalities: A Rapid Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials |journal=Healthcare |language=en |volume=12 |issue=12 |page=1217 |doi=10.3390/healthcare12121217 |doi-access=free |pmid=38921331 |pmc=11203162 }}</ref>

Two important areas of telerehabilitation research are (1) demonstrating equivalence of assessment and therapy to in-person assessment and therapy and (2) building new data collection systems to digitize information that a therapist can use in practice. Ground-breaking research in [[telehaptics]] (the sense of touch) and virtual reality may broaden the scope of telerehabilitation practice in the future.

In the United States, the [[National Institute on Disability and Rehabilitation Research]]'s (NIDRR)<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/osers/nidrr/index.html?src=mr|title=OSERS|website=www.ed.gov|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20031011114426/http://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/osers/nidrr/index.html?src=mr|archive-date=2003-10-11}}</ref> supports research and the development of telerehabilitation. NIDRR's grantees include the "Rehabilitation Engineering and Research Center" (RERC) at the [[University of Pittsburgh]], the [[Rehabilitation Institute of Chicago]], the State University of New York at Buffalo, and the National Rehabilitation Hospital in [[Washington, D.C.|Washington, D.C]]. Other federal funders of research are the [[Veterans Health Administration]], the Health Services Research Administration in the US Department of Health and Human Services, and the [[United States Department of Defense|Department of Defense]].<ref>{{cite web| vauthors = Hiers M | title = Everything You Need to Know About Telemedicine| date = 17 June 2014| url = http://www.accessrx.com/blog/current-health-news/everything-you-need-to-know-about-telemedicine-m0525/| access-date = 10 July 2014 }}</ref> Outside the United States, excellent research is conducted in [[Australia]] and [[Europe]].

Only a few [[Health insurance|health insurers]] in the United States, and about half of [[Medicaid]] programs,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Palsbo SE | title = Medicaid payment for telerehabilitation | journal = Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation | volume = 85 | issue = 7 | pages = 1188–1191 | date = July 2004 | pmid = 15241772 | doi = 10.1016/j.apmr.2003.09.008 }}</ref> [[reimburse]] for telerehabilitation services. If the research shows that teleassessments and teletherapy are equivalent to clinical encounters, it is more likely that [[insurer]]s and [[Medicare (United States)|Medicare]] will cover telerehabilitation services.

=== Teletrauma care ===
Telemedicine can be utilized to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of care delivery in a trauma environment. Examples include:

Telemedicine for trauma triage: using telemedicine, trauma specialists can interact with personnel on the scene of a mass casualty or disaster situation via the internet using mobile devices to determine the severity of injuries. They can provide clinical assessments and determine whether those injured must be evacuated for necessary care. Remote trauma specialists can provide the same quality of clinical assessment and plan of care as a trauma specialist located physically with the patient.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Collins H | title = Advanced First Responder and Medical Capabilities Could Save Lives | journal = Emergency Management | date = 28 August 2008 | url = http://www.emergencymgmt.com/disaster/Advanced-First-Responder-and.html | access-date = 23 June 2019 | archive-date = 18 August 2016 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160818095412/http://www.emergencymgmt.com/disaster/Advanced-First-Responder-and.html }}</ref>

Telemedicine for [[intensive care unit]] (ICU) rounds: Telemedicine is also being used in some trauma ICUs to reduce the spread of infections. Rounds are usually conducted at hospitals across the country by a team of approximately ten or more people including attending physicians, fellows, residents, and other clinicians. This group usually moves from bed to bed in a unit, discussing each patient. This aids in the transition of care for patients from the night shift to the morning shift but also serves as an educational experience for new residents to the team. A new approach features the team conducting rounds from a conference room using a video-conferencing system. The trauma attending, residents, fellows, nurses, nurse practitioners, and pharmacists are able to watch a live video stream from the patient's bedside. They can see the vital signs on the monitor, view the settings on the respiratory ventilator, and/or view the patient's wounds. Video-conferencing allows remote viewers to conduct two-way communication with clinicians at the bedside.<ref>{{cite web | title = Advanced technologies and wireless telecommunications enhance care and medical training at the Ryder Trauma Center in Miami | publisher = Virtual Medical Worlds | date = 4 December 2008 | url = http://www.hoise.com/vmw/09/articles/vmw/LV-VM-01-09-10.html | access-date = 23 July 2013}}</ref>

Telemedicine for trauma education: some trauma centers are delivering trauma education lectures to hospitals and health care providers worldwide using video conferencing technology. Each lecture provides fundamental principles, first-hand knowledge, and evidenced-based methods for critical analysis of established clinical practice standards, and comparisons to newer advanced alternatives. The various sites collaborate and share their perspective based on location, available staff, and available resources.<ref>{{cite web| title = EMS Trauma Grand Rounds| publisher = Utah Telehealth Network| access-date = 23 July 2013| url = http://www.utahtelehealth.net/education/ems_trauma.html| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090916083826/http://www.utahtelehealth.net/education/ems_trauma.html| archive-date = 16 September 2009}}</ref>

Telemedicine in the trauma operating room: trauma surgeons are able to observe and consult on cases from a remote location using video conferencing. This capability allows the attending to view the residents in real time. The remote surgeon has the capability to control the camera (pan, tilt, and zoom) to get the best angle of the procedure while at the same time providing expertise in order to provide the best possible care to the patient.<ref>{{cite news | vauthors = Gonzalez D | title = UM Doctors Use Telemedicine to Continue Care In Iraq | date = 10 November 2011 | url = http://www.nbcmiami.com/news/local/UM-Doctors-Use-Tele-133650778.html | access-date = 23 July 2013}}</ref>

=== Telecardiology ===
ECGs, or [[Electrocardiography|electrocardiographs]], can be transmitted using telephone and wireless. [[Willem Einthoven]], the inventor of the ECG, actually did tests with the transmission of ECG via telephone lines. This was because the hospital did not allow him to move patients outside the hospital to his laboratory for testing of his new device. In 1906, Einthoven came up with a way to transmit the data from the hospital directly to his lab.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20100826163357/http://www.medetel.lu/download/2009/parallel_sessions/presentation/day1/telecardiology_and_tele-ecg_network.pdf Telecardiology].</ref><ref>General health care delivery. Remotely treating ventricular fibrillation. Medphone Corporation, 1989{{vs|date=July 2025}}</ref>

==== Transmission of ECGs ====
One of the oldest known telecardiology systems for teletransmissions of ECGs was established in Gwalior, India, in 1975 at GR Medical College by Ajai Shanker, S. Makhija, P.K. Mantri using an indigenous technique for the first time in India.

This system enabled wireless transmission of ECG from the moving ICU van or the patients home to the central station in ICU of the department of Medicine. Transmission using wireless was done using frequency modulation which eliminated noise. Transmission was also done through telephone lines. The ECG output was connected to the telephone input using a modulator that converted ECG into high-frequency sound. At the other end a demodulator reconverted the sound into ECG with a good gain accuracy. The ECG was converted to sound waves with a frequency varying from 500 Hz to 2500 Hz with 1500 Hz at baseline.

This system was also used to monitor patients with pacemakers in remote areas. The central control unit at the ICU was able to correctly interpret [[arrhythmia]]. This technique helped medical aid reach in remote areas.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Shanker A, Makhija S, Mantri PK | title = Teletransmission of ECG Waveform: An Ingenious Low Priced Technique | journal = Indian Heart Journal | year = 1982 | volume = 34 | number = 6}}</ref>

In addition, [[Stethoscope#Electronic|electronic stethoscopes]] can be used as recording devices, which is helpful for purposes of telecardiology. There are many examples of successful telecardiology services worldwide.

In [[Pakistan]], three pilot projects in telemedicine were initiated by the Ministry of IT & Telecom, Government of Pakistan (MoIT) through the Electronic Government Directorate in collaboration with Oratier Technologies (a pioneer company within Pakistan dealing with healthcare and HMIS) and PakDataCom (a bandwidth provider). Three hub stations through were linked via the Pak Sat-I communications satellite, and four districts were linked with another hub. A 312 Kb link was also established with remote sites and 1 Mbit/s bandwidth was provided at each hub. Three hubs were established: the Mayo Hospital (the largest hospital in Asia), JPMC Karachi, and Holy Family Rawalpindi. These 12 remote sites were connected and an average of 1,500 patients were treated per month per hub. The project was still running smoothly after two years.<ref>{{cite web |title=Remote Patient Monitoring at Mayo Hospital |url=https://www.who.int/activities/promoting-telehealth |website=World Health Organization |access-date=2026-04-11}}</ref>


[[Wireless ambulatory ECG|Wireless ambulatory ECG technology]], moving beyond previous ambulatory ECG technology such as the [[Holter monitor]], now includes smartphones and [[Apple Watch|Apple Watches]], which can perform at-home cardiac monitoring and send the data to a physician via the Internet.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sanders |first1=David |last2=Ungar |first2=Leo |last3=Eskander |first3=Michael A. |last4=Seto |first4=Arnold H. |title=Ambulatory ECG monitoring in the age of smartphones |journal=Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine |date=July 2019 |volume=86 |issue=7 |pages=483–493 |doi=10.3949/ccjm.86a.18123 |doi-access=free |pmid=31291182 }}</ref>

=== Teleradiology ===
{{main|Teleradiology}}

[[File:CT viewer Chest Keosys.JPG|right|thumb|A CT exam displayed through teleradiology]]

Teleradiology is the ability to send [[Radiography|radiographic]] images ([[X-ray]]s, CT, MR, PET/CT, SPECT/CT, MG, US...) from one location to another.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kontaxakis G, Visvikis D, Ohl R, Sachpazidis I, Suarez JP, Selby P, Cheze-Le Rest C, Santos A, Ortega F, Diaz J, Pan L, Strauss L, Dimitrakopoulou-Strauss A, Sakas G, Pozo MA | title = Integrated telemedicine applications and services for oncological positron emission tomography | journal = Oncology Reports | volume = 15 | issue = 4 | pages = 1091–1100 | year = 2006 | pmid = 16525707 | doi = 10.3892/or.15.4.1091 | doi-access = free }}</ref> For this process to be implemented, three essential components are required: an image-sending station, a transmission network, and a receiving-image review station. The most typical implementation is two computers connected via the Internet. The computer at the receiving end will need a high-quality display screen that has been tested and cleared for clinical purposes. Sometimes the receiving computer will have a printer for convenience.

The teleradiology process begins at the image-sending station. The radiographic image and a modem or other connection are required for this first step. The image is scanned and then sent via the network connection to the receiving computer.

Today's high-speed broadband-based Internet enables the use of new technologies for teleradiology: the image reviewer can now have access to distant servers in order to view an exam. Therefore, they do not need particular workstations to view the images; a standard [[personal computer]] (PC) and [[digital subscriber line]] (DSL) connection is enough to reach Keosys' central server. No particular software is necessary on the PC, and the images can be reached from anywhere in the world.

Teleradiology is the most popular use for telemedicine and accounts for at least 50% of all telemedicine usage.

=== Telepathology ===
{{main|Telepathology}}

Telepathology is the practice of [[pathology]] at a distance. It uses [[telecommunications|telecommunications technology]] to facilitate the transfer of image-rich pathology data between distant locations for the purposes of [[Medical diagnosis|diagnosis]], [[Medical education|education]], and [[Medical research|research]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Weinstein RS, Graham AR, Richter LC, Barker GP, Krupinski EA, Lopez AM, Erps KA, Bhattacharyya AK, Yagi Y, Gilbertson JR | title = Overview of telepathology, virtual microscopy, and whole slide imaging: prospects for the future | journal = Human Pathology | volume = 40 | issue = 8 | pages = 1057–1069 | date = August 2009 | pmid = 19552937 | doi = 10.1016/j.humpath.2009.04.006 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Kumar S | title = Telepathology | chapter = Telepathology: An Audit | veditors = Kumar S, Dunn BE | publisher = Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg | year = 2009 | pages = 225–229| doi = 10.1007/978-3-540-85786-0_16 | isbn = 978-3-540-85785-3 }}</ref> The performance of telepathology requires that a pathologist selects the [[video]] images for analysis and rendering diagnoses. The use of "[[microscopy|television microscopy]]", the forerunner of telepathology, did not require that a pathologist have physical or virtual "hands-on" involvement in the selection of microscopic fields of view for analysis and diagnosis.

A pathologist, Ronald S. Weinstein, M.D., coined the term "telepathology" in 1986. In an editorial in a medical journal, Weinstein outlined the actions that would be needed to create remote pathology diagnostic services.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Weinstein RS | title = Prospects for telepathology | journal = Human Pathology | volume = 17 | issue = 5 | pages = 433–434 | date = May 1986 | pmid = 3516858 | doi = 10.1016/s0046-8177(86)80028-4 }}</ref> He and his diagnostic services | journal = Archives of Pathology & Laboratory Medicine | volume = 111 | issue = 7 | pages = 646–652 | date = July 1987 | pmid = 3606341 }}</ref> Weinstein was also granted the first U.S. [[patents]] for [[robotics|robotic]] telepathology systems and telepathology diagnostic networks.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kayser |first1=Klaus |last2=Szymas |first2=Janusz |last3=Weinstein |first3=Ronald S. |title=Telepathology: Telecommunication, Electronic Education and Publication in Pathology |date=1999 |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-540-65245-8 }}{{pn|date=July | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120306060350/http://www.union.edu/N/DS/s.php?s=8942 | archive-date = 6 March 2012 | access-date = 25 July 2013}}</ref> In [[Norway]], Eide and Nordrum A number of clinical telepathology services have benefited many thousands of patients in North America, Europe, and Asia.

Telepathology has been successfully used for many applications, including the rendering [[histopathology]] tissue diagnoses at a distance, for education and research. Although [[digital pathology]] imaging, including [[virtual microscopy]], is the mode of choice for telepathology services in developed countries, [[Analog signal|analog]] telepathology imaging is still used for patient services in some [[Developing country|developing countries]].

=== Teleophthalmology ===
{{main|Teleophthalmology}}

Teleophthalmology is a branch of telemedicine that delivers eye care through digital medical equipment and telecommunications technology. Today, applications of teleophthalmology encompass access to eye specialists for patients in remote areas, ophthalmic disease screening, diagnosis and monitoring; as well as distant learning. Teleophthalmology may help reduce disparities by providing remote, low-cost screening tests such as diabetic retinopathy screening to low-income and uninsured patients.<ref>{{cite web |publisher=Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality |url=https://innovations.ahrq.gov/profiles/telemedicine-based-eye-examinations-enhance-access-reduce-costs-and-increase-satisfaction |title=Telemedicine-Based Eye Examinations Enhance Access, Reduce Costs, and Increase Satisfaction for Low-Income and Minority Patients with Diabetes |date=2013-07-17 |access-date=24 July 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |publisher=Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality |url=https://innovations.ahrq.gov/profiles/remote-retinal-screening-facilitates-diagnosis-and-treatment-retinopathy-poor-andor |title=Remote Retinal Screening Facilitates Diagnosis and Treatment of Retinopathy for Poor and/or Uninsured Patients With Diabetes in Rural California |date=2012-10-03 |access-date=24 July 2013}}</ref> In Mizoram, India, a hilly area with poor roads, between 2011 and 2015, teleophthalmology provided care to over 10,000 patients. These patients were examined by ophthalmic assistants locally but surgery was done on appointment after the patient images were viewed online by eye surgeons in the hospital 6–12 hours away. Instead of an average five trips for say, a cataract procedure, only one was required for surgery alone as even post-op care like removal of stitches and appointments for glasses was done locally. There were large cost savings in travel as well.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Phukan |first1=Riki |last2=Mehta |first2=Manoj Rai |last3=Gogia |first3=Shashi |title=Results and Problems in Executing Teleophthalmology |journal=Indian Journal of Medical Informatics |volume=8 |issue=2 |date=2014 |pages=32–33 }}</ref>

In the United States, some companies allow patients to complete an online visual exam and within 24 hours receive a prescription from an optometrist valid for eyeglasses, contact lenses, or both. Some US states such as Indiana have attempted to ban these companies from doing business.<ref name=Alb>{{cite web|title=Telehealth company sues Indiana for ban on online eye exams|work=TimesUnion.com|url=https://www.timesunion.com/news/article/Telehealth-company-sues-Indiana-for-ban-on-online-13783679.php|date=21 April 2019}}</ref>

=== Telesurgery ===
{{main|Remote surgery}}

{{See also|Augmented reality-assisted surgery}}
[[Remote surgery]] (also known as telesurgery) is the ability for a doctor to perform [[surgery]] on a patient even though they are not physically in the same location. It is a form of [[telepresence]]. Remote surgery combines elements of [[robot]]ics, cutting-edge [[telecommunication]]s such as high-speed data connections, [[telehaptics]] and elements of [[management information system]]s. While the field of [[robotic surgery]] is fairly well established, most of these robots are controlled by surgeons at the location of the surgery.

Remote surgery is [[remote work]] for surgeons, where the physical distance between the surgeon and the patient is immaterial. It promises to allow the expertise of specialized surgeons to be available to patients worldwide, without the need for patients to travel beyond their local hospital.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.intersurgtech.com/media.html | title=IST's Media Collection | work=Interface Surgical Technologies}}</ref>

Remote surgery or telesurgery is performance of surgical procedures where the surgeon is not physically in the same location as the patient, using a robotic [[teleoperator]] system controlled by the surgeon. The remote operator may give tactile feedback to the user. Remote surgery combines elements of robotics and high-speed data connections. A critical limiting factor is the speed, [[Latency (engineering)|latency]] and reliability of the communication system between the surgeon and the patient, though trans-Atlantic surgeries have been demonstrated.

=== Teleabortion ===
Telemedicine has been used globally to increase access to abortion care, specifically [[medical abortion]], in environments where few abortion care providers exist or abortion is legally restricted. Clinicians are able to virtually provide counseling, review screening tests, observe the administration of an abortion medication, and directly mail abortion pills to people.<ref name="Endler-2019">{{cite journal | vauthors = Endler M, Lavelanet A, Cleeve A, Ganatra B, Gomperts R, Gemzell-Danielsson K | title = Telemedicine for medical abortion: a systematic review | journal = BJOG | volume = 126 | issue = 9 | pages = 1094–1102 | date = August 2019 | pmid = 30869829 | pmc = 7496179 | doi = 10.1111/1471-0528.15684 | doi-access = free }}</ref> In 2004, [[Women on Web]] (WoW), Amsterdam, started offering online consultations, mostly to people living in areas where abortion was legally restricted, informing them how to safely use medical abortion drugs to end a pregnancy.<ref name="Endler-2019" /> People contact the Women on Web service online; physicians review any necessary lab results or ultrasounds, mail [[mifepristone]] and [[misoprostol]] pills to people, then follow up through online communication.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Study: Taking abortion pill at home as safe as in a clinic|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/women-safely-take-abortion-pills-home-online-consult-n760576|website=NBC News|date=17 May 2017 |language=en|access-date=2020-05-18}}</ref> In the United States, [[medical abortion]] was introduced as a telehealth service in Iowa by Planned Parenthood of the Heartland in 2008 to allow a patient at one health facility to communicate via secure video with a health provider at another facility.<ref name="Guttmacher Institute-2019">{{Cite web|title=Improving Access to Abortion via Telehealth|url=https://www.guttmacher.org/gpr/2019/05/improving-access-abortion-telehealth|date=2019-05-07|website=Guttmacher Institute|language=en|access-date=2020-04-21}}</ref> In this model a person seeking abortion care must come to a health facility. An abortion care provider communicates with the person located at another site using clinic-to-clinic videoconferencing to provide medical abortion after screening tests and consultation with clinic staff. In 2018, the website [[Aid Access]] was launched by the founder of Women on Web, [[Rebecca Gomperts]]. It offers a similar service as Women on Web in the United States, but the medications are prescribed to an Indian pharmacy, then mailed to the United States.

The TelAbortion study conducted by Gynuity Health Projects, with special approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), aims to increase access to medical abortion care without requiring an in-person visit to a clinic.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Telabortion Project|url=https://telabortion.org/about/|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref><ref name="Belluck-2020">{{Cite news| vauthors = Belluck P |title=Abortion by Telemedicine: A Growing Option as Access to Clinics Wanes|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=28 April 2020 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/04/28/health/telabortion-abortion-telemedicine.html|access-date=May 5, 2020}}</ref><ref name="Guttmacher Institute-2019" /> This models was expanded during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] and as of March 2020 exists in 13 U.S. states and has enrolled over 730 people in the study.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Home - Telabortion|url=https://telabortion.org/|website=telabortion.org|access-date=2020-05-11}}</ref><ref name="Belluck-2020" /> The person receives counseling and instruction from an abortion care provider via videoconference from a location of their choice. The medications necessary for the abortion, mifepristone and misoprostol, are mailed directly to the person and they have a follow-up video consultation in 7–14 days. A systematic review of telemedicine abortion has found the practice to be safe, effective, efficient, and satisfactory.<ref name="Endler-2019" />

In the United States, eighteen states require the clinician to be physically present during the administration of medications for abortion which effectively bans telehealth of medication abortion: five states explicitly ban telemedicine for medication abortion, while thirteen states require the prescriber (usually required to be a physician) to be physically present with the patient.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Jones RK, Jerman J | title = Abortion Incidence and Service Availability In the United States, 2014 | journal = Perspectives on Sexual and Reproductive Health | volume = 49 | issue = 1 | pages = 17–27 | date = March 2017 | pmid = 28094905 | pmc = 5487028 | doi = 10.1363/2019.30760 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-06-08|title=Medication Abortion and Telemedicine: Innovations and Barriers During the COVID-19 Emergency|url=https://www.kff.org/policy-watch/medication-abortion-telemedicine-innovations-and-barriers-during-the-covid-19-emergency/|access-date=2020-08-03|website=KFF|language=en-US}}</ref> In the UK, the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists approved a no-test protocol for medication abortion, with mifepristone available through a minimal-contact pick-up or by mail.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Coronavirus (COVID-19) infection and abortion care|url=https://www.rcog.org.uk/en/guidelines-research-services/guidelines/coronavirus-abortion/|access-date=2020-08-03|website=Royal College of Obstetricians & Gynaecologists|language=en-US}}</ref>

== Major developments ==

=== In policy ===
Telehealth is a modern form of health care delivery. Telehealth breaks away from traditional health care delivery by using modern telecommunication systems including wireless communication methods.<ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Altharthi |first1=Mansour Saeed |title=Telehealth practice in eight countries: New Zealand, Australia, the USA, Canada, UK, Malaysia, China and India: a thesis presented in partial fulfillment of the requirements of degree of Master in Information Science at Massey University, Albany campus, Auckland, New Zealand |date=2012 |hdl=10179/3538 |hdl-access=free |oclc=1085527078 }}{{pn|date=July 2025}}</ref><ref name="García-Rojo-2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = García-Rojo M | title = International Clinical Guidelines for the Adoption of Digital Pathology: A Review of Technical Aspects | journal = Pathobiology | volume = 83 | issue = 2–3 | pages = 99–109 | pmid = 27100834 | doi = 10.1159/000441192 | year = 2016 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Traditional health is legislated through policy to ensure the safety of medical practitioners and patients. Consequently, since telehealth is a new form of health care delivery that is now gathering momentum in the health sector, many organizations have started to legislate the use of telehealth into policy.<ref name="García-Rojo-2016" /> In New Zealand, the Medical Council has a statement about telehealth on their website. This illustrates that the medical council has foreseen the importance that telehealth will have on the health system and have started to introduce telehealth legislation to practitioners along with government.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.mcnz.org.nz/assets/News-and-Publications/Statement-on-telehealthv3.pdf |title=Statement on telehealth | date=2013 |publisher=Medical Council of New Zealand }}</ref>

=== Transition to mainstream ===
{{See also|Remote patient monitoring}}

Traditional use of telehealth services has been for specialist treatment. However, there has been a paradigm shift and telehealth is no longer considered a specialist service.<ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Lucas |first1=Julie Anne |title=Clinicians' Perceptions of Telemedicine: Opportunities and Barriers for Emergency Medicine |date=2013 |hdl=2292/20430 |hdl-access=free }}{{pn|date=July 2025}}</ref> This development has ensured that many access barriers are eliminated, as medical professionals and patients are able to use wireless communication technologies to deliver health care.<ref name="Bazzano-2024">{{Cite journal |last1=Bazzano |first1=Alessandra N. |last2=Patel |first2=Tejal |last3=Nauman |first3=Elizabeth |last4=Cernigliaro |first4=Dana |last5=Shi |first5=Lizheng |date=2024-01-01 |title=Optimizing Telehealth for Diabetes Management in the Deep South of the United States: Qualitative Study of Barriers and Facilitators on the Patient and Clinician Journey |journal=Journal of Medical Internet Research |language=EN |volume=26 |issue=1 |article-number=e43583 |doi=10.2196/43583|doi-access=free |pmid=37976468 |pmc=10790202 }}</ref> This is evident in [[Rural health|rural communities]]. Rural residents typically have to travel to longer distances to access healthcare than urban counterparts due to physician shortages and healthcare facility closures in these areas.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Transportation to Support Rural Healthcare Overview - Rural Health Information Hub |url=https://www.ruralhealthinfo.org/topics/transportation#travel-burdens |access-date=2024-04-14 |website=www.ruralhealthinfo.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Healthcare Access in Rural Communities Overview - Rural Health Information Hub |url=https://www.ruralhealthinfo.org/topics/healthcare-access |access-date=2024-04-14 |website=www.ruralhealthinfo.org |language=en}}</ref> Telehealth eliminates this barrier as health professionals are able to conduct medical consultations through the use of wireless communication technologies. However, this process is dependent on both parties having internet access and comfort level with technology, which poses barriers for many low-income and rural communities.<ref name="Bazzano-2024" /><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Possemato K, Bishop TM, Willis MA, Lantinga LJ | title = Healthcare utilization and symptom variation among veterans using Behavioral Telehealth Center services | journal = The Journal of Behavioral Health Services & Research | volume = 40 | issue = 4 | pages = 416–26 | date = October 2013 | pmid = 23616251 | doi = 10.1007/s11414-013-9338-y }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Darkins A, Foster L, Anderson C, Goldschmidt L, Selvin G | title = The design, implementation, and operational management of a comprehensive quality management program to support national telehealth networks | journal = Telemedicine Journal and e-Health | volume = 19 | issue = 7 | pages = 557–64 | date = July 2013 | pmid = 23705961 | doi = 10.1089/tmj.2012.0263 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Telehealth and Health Information Technology in Rural Healthcare Overview - Rural Health Information Hub |url=https://www.ruralhealthinfo.org/topics/telehealth-health-it#:~:text=Challenges%20for%20providing%20telehealth%20services,and%20access%20to%20broadband%20services. |access-date=2024-04-14 |website=www.ruralhealthinfo.org |language=en}}</ref>

Telehealth allows the patient to be monitored between physician office visits which can improve patient health. Telehealth also allows patients to access expertise which is not available in their local area. This remote patient monitoring ability enables patients to stay at home longer and helps avoid unnecessary hospital time. In the long-term, this could potentially result in less burdening of the healthcare system and consumption of resources.<ref name="Office for the Advancement of Telehealth-2022" /><ref name="Maheu-2002" />

During the COVID-19 pandemic, there were large increases in the use of telemedicine for primary care visits within the United States, increasing from an average of 1.4 million visits in Q2 of 2018 and 2019 to 35 million visits in Q2 2020, according to data from [[IQVIA]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Alexander GC, Tajanlangit M, Heyward J, Mansour O, Qato DM, Stafford RS | title = Use and Content of Primary Care Office-Based vs Telemedicine Care Visits During the COVID-19 Pandemic in the US | journal = JAMA Network Open | volume = 3 | issue = 10 | pages = e2021476 | date = October 2020 | pmid = 33006622 | pmc = 7532385 | doi = 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2020.21476  | doi-access = free}}</ref> The telehealth market is expected to grow at 40% a year in 2021. Use of telemedicine by General Practitioners in the UK rose from 20 to 30% pre-COVID to almost 80% by the beginning of 2021. More than 70% of practitioners and patients were satisfied with this.<ref>{{cite news |title=Telemedicine is here to stay |url=https://www.buildingbetterhealthcare.com/news/article_page/Telemedicine_is_here_to_stay/178218/cn164706 |access-date=26 September 2021 |publisher=Building Better Healthcare |date=11 August 2021}}</ref> [[Boris Johnson]] was said to have "piled pressure on GPs to offer more in-person consultations" supporting a campaign largely orchestrated by the ''[[Daily Mail]]''. The [[Royal College of General Practitioners]] said that a patient "right" to have face-to-face appointments if they wish was "undeliverable".<ref>{{cite news |title=Prime Minister says GPs should see patients face to face |url=https://www.pulsetoday.co.uk/news/breaking-news/prime-minister-says-gps-should-see-patients-face-to-face/ |access-date=26 September 2021 |publisher=Pulse |date=21 September 2021}}</ref>

=== Technology advancement ===
{{See also|Technology|Emerging technologies}}

The technological advancement of wireless communication devices is a major development in telehealth.<ref name="Vockley-2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Vockley M | title = The Rise of Telehealth: 'Triple Aim,' Innovative Technology, and Popular Demand Are Spearheading New Models of Health and Wellness Care | journal = Biomedical Instrumentation & Technology | volume = 49 | issue = 5 | pages = 306–20 | date = 2015-10-01 | pmid = 26443907 | doi = 10.2345/0899-8205-49.5.306 }}</ref> This allows patients to self-monitor their health conditions and to not rely as much on health care professionals. Furthermore, patients are more willing to stay on their treatment plans as they are more invested and included in the process as the decision-making is shared.<ref name="Kvedar-2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kvedar J, Coye MJ, Everett W | title = Connected health: a review of technologies and strategies to improve patient care with telemedicine and telehealth | journal = Health Affairs | volume = 33 | issue = 2 | pages = 194–9 | date = February 2014 | pmid = 24493760 | doi = 10.1377/hlthaff.2013.0992 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="Hirani-2017">{{cite journal |last1=Hirani |first1=Shashivadan P |last2=Rixon |first2=Lorna |last3=Beynon |first3=Michelle |last4=Cartwright |first4=Martin |last5=Cleanthous |first5=Sophie |last6=Selva |first6=Abi |last7=Sanders |first7=Caroline |last8=Newman |first8=Stanton P |last9=WSD |first9=investigators |title=Quantifying beliefs regarding telehealth: Development of the Whole Systems Demonstrator Service User Technology Acceptability Questionnaire |journal=Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare |date=May 2017 |volume=23 |issue=4 |pages=460–469 |doi=10.1177/1357633X16649531 |pmid=27224997 }}</ref> Technological advancement also means that health care professionals are able to use better technologies to treat patients for example in maternal care<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Cantor AG, Jungbauer RM, Totten AM, Tilden EL, Holmes R, Ahmed A, Wagner J, Hermesch AC, McDonagh MS | title = Telehealth Strategies for the Delivery of Maternal Health Care: A Rapid Review | journal = Annals of Internal Medicine | volume = 175 | issue = 9 | pages = 1285–1297 | date = September 2022 | pmid = 35878405 | doi = 10.7326/M22-0737 }}</ref> and [[surgery]]. A 2023 study published in the ''[[Journal of the American College of Surgeons]]'' showed telemedicine as making a positive impact, with expectations exceeded for those physicians and patients who had consulted online for surgeries.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.medicaleconomics.com/view/telemedicine-better-than-expected-for-consulting-on-surgeries|author=Richard Payerchin|title=Telemedicine better than expected for consulting on surgeries|website=Medical Economics|date=January 20, 2023}}</ref> Technological developments in telehealth are essential to improve health care, especially the delivery of healthcare services, as resources are finite along with an ageing population that is living longer.<ref name="Vockley-2015" /><ref name="Kvedar-2014" /><ref name="Hirani-2017" />

== Licensing ==
=== U.S. licensing and regulatory issues ===
Restrictive licensure laws in the United States require a practitioner to obtain a full license to deliver telemedicine care across state lines. Typically, states with restrictive licensure laws also have several exceptions (varying from state to state) that may release an out-of-state practitioner from the additional burden of obtaining such a license. A number of states require practitioners who seek compensation to frequently deliver interstate care to acquire a full license.

If a practitioner serves several states, obtaining this license in each state could be an expensive and time-consuming proposition. Even if the practitioner never practices medicine face-to-face with a patient in another state, he/she still must meet a variety of other individual state requirements, including paying substantial licensure fees, passing additional oral and written examinations, and traveling for interviews.

In 2008, the U.S. passed the Ryan Haight Act which required face-to-face or valid telemedicine consultations prior to receiving a prescription.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.govtech.com/health/Ryan-Haight-Act-will.html|title=Ryan Haight Act will Require Tighter Restrictions on Internet Pharmacies|website=www.govtech.com|date=27 July 2010|access-date=7 March 2016}}</ref>

[[:Category:Medical licensing boards in the United States|State medical licensing boards]] have sometimes opposed telemedicine; for example, in 2012 electronic consultations were illegal in Idaho, and an Idaho-licensed general practitioner was punished by the board for prescribing an antibiotic, triggering reviews of her licensure and board certifications across the country.<ref name=":0b">{{cite web|url=http://www.spokesman.com/stories/2015/aug/22/telemedicine-sanction-in-idaho-clouds-doctors/|title=Telemedicine sanction in Idaho clouds doctor's future|website=Spokesman.com|access-date=7 March 2016}}</ref> Subsequently, in 2015 the state legislature legalized electronic consultations.<ref name=":0b" />

In 2015, Teladoc filed suit against the [[Texas Medical Board]] over a rule that required in-person consultations initially; the judge refused to dismiss the case, noting that antitrust laws apply to state medical boards.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.modernhealthcare.com/article/20151214/NEWS/151219924|title=Teladoc case against Texas Medical Board will move forward, judge rules|website=Modern Healthcare|date=14 December 2015|access-date=7 March 2016}}</ref>

=== EU licensing and regulatory issues ===
In the European Union, telemedicine service providers are primarily subject to the regulatory requirements that apply at their place of establishment (country of origin principle).<ref>{{cite SSRN |last1=Hahn |first1=Erik |last2=Liddell |first2=Kathleen |last3=Aboy |first3=Mateo |last4=Cohen |first4=I. Glenn |title=Cross-border telemedicine - A reason to 'smile'? also comment on ECJ, judgment of 11 September 2025 -C-115/24 (UJ/Austrian Dental Association) |date=24 November 2025 |ssrn=5798224 |ssrn-access=free}}</ref>

== Major implications and impacts ==
Telehealth allows multiple, varying disciplines to merge and deliver a potentially more uniform level of care, using technology. As telehealth proliferates mainstream healthcare, it challenges notions of traditional healthcare delivery. Some populations experience better quality, access and more personalized health care.<ref name="Elsevier-2012">{{Cite book|title=Telemental Health: Clinical, Technical, and Administrative Foundations for Evidence-Based Practice|date=2012-09-20|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=978-0-12-416048-4 | veditors = Myers K, Turvey C |edition=1  }}</ref><ref name="Umefjord-2006">{{cite thesis |last1=Umefjord |first1=Göran |title=Internet consultation in medicine: studies of a text-based Ask the doctor service |date=2006 |url=https://urn.kb.se/resolve?urn=urn:nbn:se:umu:diva-854 }}{{pn|date=July 2025}}</ref>

{{See also|Health care quality}}

A [[scientific review]] indicates that, in general, outcomes of telemedicine are or can be as good as in-person care with health care use staying similar.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Albritton J, Ortiz A, Wines R, Booth G, DiBello M, Brown S, Gartlehner G, Crotty K | title = Video Teleconferencing for Disease Prevention, Diagnosis, and Treatment: A Rapid Review | journal = Annals of Internal Medicine | volume = 175 | issue = 2 | pages = 256–266 | date = February 2022 | pmid = 34871056 | doi = 10.7326/m21-3511 }}</ref>

Theoretically, the whole health system could benefit from telehealth. There are indications telehealth consumes fewer resources and requires fewer people to operate it with shorter training periods to implement initiatives.<ref name="The Center for Connected Health Policy" /> Commenters suggested that lawmakers may fear that making telehealth widely accessible, without any other measures, would lead to patients using unnecessary health care services.<ref name="aafp-tele"/> Telemedicine could also be used for connected networks between health care professionals.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hyder MA, Razzak J | title = Telemedicine in the United States: An Introduction for Students and Residents | journal = Journal of Medical Internet Research | volume = 22 | issue = 11 | article-number = e20839 | date = November 2020 | pmid = 33215999 | pmc = 7690251 | doi = 10.2196/20839 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Telemedicine also can eliminate the possible transmission of [[infectious disease]]s or [[parasite]]s between patients and medical staff. This is particularly an issue where [[MRSA]] is a concern. Additionally, some patients who feel uncomfortable in a doctors office may do better remotely. For example, [[white coat syndrome]] may be avoided. Patients who are home-bound and would otherwise require an ambulance to move them to a clinic are also a consideration.
