=== Geriatric population ===

Technologies' growing involvement in health care has led to continuous improvement in access, efficiency and quality of care, but numerous challenges lie with addressing the barriers that impair the geriatric population from benefitting from the use of this new technology.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alverson |first1=Dale C. |last2=Krupinski |first2=Elizabeth A. |last3=Erps |first3=Kristine A. |last4=Rowe |first4=Nancy S. |last5=Weinstein |first5=Ronald S. |title=The Third National Telemedicine & Telehealth Service Provider Showcase Conference: Advancing Telehealth Partnerships |journal=Telemedicine and e-Health |date=April 2019 |volume=25 |issue=4 |pages=332–340 |doi=10.1089/tmj.2018.0096 |pmid=29851367 |pmc=6482893 }}</ref> With the COVID-19 pandemic, rapid implementation of telehealth in geriatric outpatient clinics occurred. Although time efficiency greatly improved and increased access to geriatric patients with lack of transportation to the clinic, there were complications that arose during and after implementation with many appointments requiring rescheduling due to language barrier, poor connection, hard of hearing, or inability to perform assessments.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Callisaya |first1=Michele L. |last2=Lee |first2=Angel Hui-Ching |last3=Khushu |first3=Anjali |title=Rapid implementation of telehealth in geriatric outpatient clinics due to COVID-19 |journal=Internal Medicine Journal |date=July 2021 |volume=51 |issue=7 |pages=1151–1155 |doi=10.1111/imj.15306 |pmid=34143563 |pmc=8444941 }}</ref> Studies also show that patients and their family member often preferred in-person visits. Even though patients were able to meet with a provider sooner and had access to high-quality audio and video as well as family participation during visits, patients and family noted preferences for in-person visits due to the difficulty in using the service.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Groom |first1=Lisa L. |last2=McCarthy |first2=Margaret M. |last3=Stimpfel |first3=Amy Witkoski |last4=Brody |first4=Abraham A. |title=Telemedicine and Telehealth in Nursing Homes: An Integrative Review |journal=Journal of the American Medical Directors Association |date=September 2021 |volume=22 |issue=9 |pages=1784–1801.e7 |doi=10.1016/j.jamda.2021.02.037 |pmid=33819450 |pmc=9626369 }}</ref> Improvements are being made to help ease the complications of telehealth for geriatric patients. These include integrated captions on video calls for the hearing impaired, virtual interpreters that will attend the calls for language differences, government assisted internet services, and increased training to medical providers and patients on telehealth use.{{citation needed|date=September 2025}}

=== Economic evaluations ===
Due to its digital nature, it is often assumed that telehealth saves the health system money. However, the evidence to support this is varied. When conducting economic evaluations of telehealth services, the individuals evaluating them need to be aware of potential outcomes and extraclinical benefits of the telehealth service.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Snoswell C, Smith AC, Scuffham PA, Whitty JA | title = Economic evaluation strategies in telehealth: Obtaining a more holistic valuation of telehealth interventions | journal = Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare | volume = 23 | issue = 9 | pages = 792–796 | date = October 2017 | pmid = 27789615 | doi = 10.1177/1357633x16671407 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Economic viability relies on the funding model within the country being examined (public vs private), the consumers willingness-to-pay, and the expected remuneration by the clinicians or commercial entities providing the services (examples of research on these topics from teledermoscopy in Australia)<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Snoswell CL, Whitty JA, Caffery LJ, Loescher LJ, Gillespie N, Janda M | title = Direct-to-consumer mobile teledermoscopy for skin cancer screening: Preliminary results demonstrating willingness-to-pay in Australia | journal = Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare | volume = 24 | issue = 10 | pages = 683–689 | date = December 2018 | pmid = 30343653 | doi = 10.1177/1357633x18799582 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Snoswell CL, Caffery LJ, Whitty JA, Soyer HP, Gordon LG | title = Cost-effectiveness of Skin Cancer Referral and Consultation Using Teledermoscopy in Australia | journal = JAMA Dermatology | volume = 154 | issue = 6 | pages = 694–700 | date = June 2018 | pmid = 29801161 | pmc = 6145645 | doi = 10.1001/jamadermatol.2018.0855 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Snoswell CL, Whitty JA, Caffery LJ, Finnane A, Soyer HP | title = What do Australian dermatologists expect to be paid for store-and-forward teledermoscopy? A preliminary investigation | journal = Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare | volume = 25 | issue = 7 | pages = 438–444 | date = August 2019 | pmid = 29933722 | doi = 10.1177/1357633x18776766 | url = https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/id/eprint/68175/1/Accepted_manuscript.pdf }}</ref>

In a UK telehealth trial done in 2011, it was reported that the cost of health could be dramatically reduced with the use of telehealth monitoring. The usual cost of [[in vitro fertilisation]] (IVF) per cycle would be around $15,000; with telehealth it was reduced to $800 per patient.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chausiaux O, Hayes J, Long C, Morris S, Williams G, Husheer S | title = Pregnancy Prognosis in Infertile Couples on the DuoFertility Programme Compared with In Vitro Fertilisation/Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection. | journal = European Obstetrics & Gynaecology | date = 2011 | volume = 6 | issue = 2 | pages = 92–94 }}</ref> In [[Alaska Federal Health Care Access Network|Alaska the Federal Health Care Access Network]], which connects 3,000 healthcare providers to communities, engaged in 160,000 telehealth consultations from 2001 and saved the state $8.5 million in travel costs for just [[Medicaid]] patients.<ref>{{cite web |date=2013 |title=Telehealth Improves Access and Quality of Care for Alaska Natives. |url=https://innovations.ahrq.gov/perspectives/telehealth-improves-access-and-quality-care-alaska-natives |work=The Innovations Exchange Team.}}</ref>

[[Use of technology in treatment of mental disorders|Digital interventions for mental health conditions]] seem to be cost-effective compared to no intervention or non-therapeutic responses such as monitoring. == Limitations and restrictions ==
While many branches of medicine have wanted to fully embrace telehealth for a long time, there are certain risks and barriers which bar the full amalgamation of telehealth into [[best practice]]. For a start, it is dubious as to whether a practitioner can fully leave the "hands-on" experience behind.<ref name="Umefjord-2006" /> Although it is predicted that telehealth will replace many consultations and other health interactions, it cannot yet fully replace a physical examination, this is particularly so in [[Medical diagnosis|diagnostics]], [[Physical medicine and rehabilitation|rehabilitation]] or [[mental health]].<ref name="Umefjord-2006" /> To minimise safety issues, researchers have suggested not offering remote consultations for some conditions (breathing problems, new psychosis, or acute chest pain, for example), when a parent is very concerned about a child, when a condition has not resolved as expected or has worsened, or to people who might struggle to understand or be understood (such as those with limited English or learning difficulties).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Payne |first1=Rebecca |last2=Clarke |first2=Aileen |last3=Swann The benefits posed by telehealth challenge the normative means of healthcare delivery set in both legislation and practice. Therefore, the growing prominence of telehealth is starting to underscore the need for updated regulations, guidelines and legislation which reflect the current and future trends of healthcare practices.<ref name="Shaw-2009" /><ref name="Umefjord-2006" /> Telehealth enables timely and flexible care to patients wherever they may be which reduces travel time; although this is a benefit, it also poses threats to [[privacy]], [[safety]] [[Medical license|, medical licensing]] and [[reimbursement]], even so it still increases healthcare access and reduces costs. When a clinician and patient are in different locations, it is difficult to determine which laws apply to the context.<ref name="pmid24820794">{{cite journal | vauthors = Keck CS, Doarn CR | title = Telehealth technology applications in speech-language pathology | journal = Telemedicine Journal and E-health | volume = 20 | issue = 7 | pages = 653–9 | date = July 2014 | pmid = 24820794 | doi = 10.1089/tmj.2013.0295 }}</ref> Once healthcare crosses borders different state bodies are involved in order to regulate and maintain the level of care that is warranted to the patient or telehealth consumer. As it stands, telehealth is complex with many grey areas when put into practice especially as it crosses borders. This effectively limits the potential benefits of telehealth.<ref name="Shaw-2009" /><ref name="Umefjord-2006" />

An example of these limitations include the current American reimbursement infrastructure, where [[Medicare (United States)|Medicare]] will reimburse for telehealth services only when a patient is living in an area where specialists are in shortage, or in particular rural counties. The area is defined by whether it is a medical facility as opposed to a patient's' home. The site that the practitioner is in, however, is unrestricted. Medicare will only reimburse live video (synchronous) type services, not store-and-forward, mhealth or remote patient monitoring (if it does not involve live-video). Some insurers currently will reimburse telehealth, but not all yet. So providers and patients must go to the extra effort of finding the correct insurers before continuing. Again in America, states generally tend to require that clinicians are licensed to practice in the surgery' state, therefore they can only provide their service if licensed in an area that they do not live in themselves.<ref name=":0b" />

More specific and widely reaching laws, legislations and regulations will have to evolve with the technology. They will have to be fully agreed upon, for example, will all clinicians need full licensing in every community they provide telehealth services too, or could there be a limited use telehealth licence? Would the limited use licence cover all potential telehealth interventions, or only some? Who would be responsible if an emergency was occurring and the practitioner could not provide immediate help – would someone else have to be in the room with the patient at all consult times? Which state, city or country would the law apply in when a breach or malpractice occurred?<ref name="Umefjord-2006" /><ref name="Paul-2006">{{cite journal |last1=Paul |first1=David L. |title=Collaborative Activities in Virtual Settings: A Knowledge Management Perspective of Telemedicine |journal=Journal of Management Information Systems |date=2006 |volume=22 |issue=4 |pages=143–176 |doi=10.2753/MIS0742-1222220406 |jstor=40398816 }}</ref>

A major legal action prompt in telehealth thus far has been issues surrounding online prescribing and whether an appropriate clinician-patient relationship can be established online to make prescribing safe, making this an area that requires particular scrutiny.<ref name="Elsevier-2012" /> It may be required that the practitioner and patient involved must meet in person at least once before online prescribing can occur, or that at least a live-video conference must occur, not just impersonal questionnaires or surveys to determine need.<ref name="Cascella-2014">{{cite magazine |last1=Cascella |first1=Laura M |title=Virtual risk: An overview of telehealth from a risk management perspective |magazine=Protector |date=Spring 2014 |pages=2–13 }}</ref>

Telehealth has some potential for facilitating self-management techniques in health care, but for patients to benefit from it, the appropriate contact with, and relationship, between doctor and patient must be established first.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Luz PL | title = Telemedicine and the Doctor/Patient Relationship | journal = Arquivos Brasileiros de Cardiologia | volume = 113 | issue = 1 | pages = 100–102 | date = August 2019 | pmid = 31411296 | pmc = 6684176 | doi = 10.5935/abc.20190117 }}</ref> This would start with an online consultation, providing patients with techniques and tools that help them participate in healthy behaviors, and initiating a collaborative partnership between health care professionals and patient.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite journal | vauthors = Dineen-Griffin S, Garcia-Cardenas V, Williams K, Benrimoj SI | title = Helping patients help themselves: A systematic review of self-management support strategies in primary health care practice | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 14 | issue = 8 | article-number = e0220116 | date = 2019-08-01 | pmid = 31369582 | pmc = 6675068 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0220116 | bibcode = 2019PLoSO..1420116D | doi-access = free | veditors = Leroyer C }}</ref> Self-management strategies fall into a broader category called patient activation, which is defined as a "patients' willingness and ability to take independent actions to manage their health."<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hibbard JH, Greene J | title = What the evidence shows about patient activation: better health outcomes and care experiences; fewer data on costs | journal = Health Affairs | volume = 32 | issue = 2 | pages = 207–214 | date = February 2013 | pmid = 23381511 | doi = 10.1377/hlthaff.2012.1061 }}</ref> It can be achieved by increasing patients' knowledge and confidence in coping with and managing their own disease through a "regular assessment of progress [...] and problem-solving support."<ref name="ReferenceA"/> Teaching patients about their conditions and ways to cope with chronic illnesses will allow them to be knowledgeable about their disease and willing to manage it, improving their everyday life. Without a focus on the doctor-patient relationship and on the patient's understanding, telehealth cannot improve the quality of life of patients, despite the benefit of allowing them to do their medical check-ups from the comfort of their home.

== Ethical issues ==
{{See also|Informed consent|Medical ethics}}

''[[Informed consent]]'' is another issue. When telehealth includes the possibility for technical problems such as transmission errors, security breaches, or storage issues, it can impact the system's ability to communicate. It may be wise to obtain informed consent in person first, as well as having backup options for when technical issues occur. In person, a patient can see who is involved in their care (namely themselves and their clinician in a consult), but online there will be other involved such as the technology providers, therefore consent may need to involve disclosure of anyone involved in the transmission of the information and the security that will keep their information private, and any legal malpractice cases may need to involve all of those involved as opposed to what would usually just be the practitioner.<ref name="Elsevier-2012" /><ref name="Paul-2006" /><ref name="Cascella-2014" />

== State of the market ==
The rate of adoption of telehealth services in any jurisdiction is frequently influenced by factors such as the adequacy and cost of existing conventional [[health care|health services]] in meeting [[patient|patient needs]]; the policies of governments and/or insurers with respect to coverage and payment for telehealth services; and medical licensing requirements that may inhibit or deter the provision of telehealth second opinions or primary consultations by physicians.

Projections for the growth of the telehealth market are optimistic, and much of this optimism is predicated upon the increasing demand for remote medical care. According to a recent survey, nearly three-quarters of U.S. consumers say they would use telehealth.<ref name="healthdata">{{cite web|url=http://www.healthdatamanagement.com/news/telemedicine-38701-1.html|title=Survey: Consumers Keen on Telemedicine|access-date=2010-04-26|archive-date=2010-04-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100429075350/http://www.healthdatamanagement.com/news/telemedicine-38701-1.html}}</ref> At present, several major companies along with a bevvy of startups are working to develop a leading presence in the field.

In the UK, the Government's Care Services minister, Paul Burstow, has stated that telehealth and [[telecare]] would be extended over the next five years (2012–2017) to reach three million people.

===United States===
In the United States, telemedicine companies are collaborating with health insurers and other telemedicine providers to expand marketshare and patient access to telemedicine consultations.

{{as of|2019}}, 95% of employers believe their organizations will continue to provide health care benefits over the next five years.<ref>''[https://www.willistowerswatson.com/en-US/Insights/2019/11/2019-best-practices-in-health-care-employer-survey-highlights 2019 Best Practices in Health Care Employer Survey Highlights]'', Willis Towers Watson, November 5, 2019</ref>

The COVID-19 pandemic drove increased usage of telehealth services in the U.S. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported a 154% increase in telehealth visits during the last week of March 2020, compared to the same dates in 2019.<ref>''[https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/wr/mm6943a3.htm?s_cid=mm6943a3_e&ACSTrackingID=USCDC_921-DM41453&ACSTrackingLabel=This%20Week%20in%20MMWR%20-%20Vol.%2069%2c%20October%2030%2c%202020&deliveryName=USCDC_921-DM41453 Trends in the Use of Telehealth During the Emergence of the COVID-19 Pandemic — United States, January–March 2020]'', Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR), October 30, 2020</ref>

=== Switzerland ===
From 1999 to 2018, the [[University Hospital of Zürich|University Hospital of Zurich]] (USZ) offered clinical telemedicine and online medical advice on the Internet. A team of doctors answered around 2500 anonymous inquiries annually, usually within 24 to 48 hours. The team consisted of up to six physicians who are specialists in clinical telemedicine at the USZ and have many years of experience, particularly in internal and general medicine. In the entire period, 59360 inquiries were sent and answered.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kessler SH, Schmidt-Weitmann S | title = Diseases and Emotions: An Automated Content Analysis of Health Narratives in Inquiries to an Online Health Consultation Service | journal = Health Communication | volume = 36 | issue = 2 | pages = 226–235 | date = February 2021 | pmid = 36112901 | doi = 10.1080/10410236.2019.1673950 | url = https://www.zora.uzh.ch/id/eprint/175841/1/Schmidt_Manuskript_Diseases_and_Emotions.pdf }}</ref> The majority of the users were female and on average 38 years old. However, in the course of time, considerably more men and older people began to use the service. The diversity of medical queries covered all categories of the [[International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems]] (ICD) and correlated with the statistical frequency of diseases in hospitals in Switzerland. Most of the inquiries concerned unclassified symptoms and signs, services related to reproduction, respiratory diseases, skin diseases, health services, diseases of the eye and nervous systems, injuries and disorders of the female genital tract. As with the Swedish online medical advice service,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Umefjord G, Sandström H, Malker H, Petersson G | title = Medical text-based consultations on the Internet: a 4-year study | journal = International Journal of Medical Informatics | volume = 77 | issue = 2 | pages = 114–121 | date = February 2008 | pmid = 17317292 | doi = 10.1016/j.ijmedinf.2007.01.009 }}</ref> one-sixth of the requests related to often shameful and [[Social stigma|stigmatised]] diseases of the genitals, gastrointestinal tract, sexually transmitted infections, obesity and mental disorders. By providing an anonymous space where users can talk about (shameful) diseases, online telemedical services empower patients and their health literacy is enhanced by providing individualized health information. In [[Europe]], several private [[telemedicine]] platforms facilitate remote consultations combined with [[Electronic prescription|prescription]] services through partner [[Pharmacy|pharmacies]].<ref>{{cite report |url= |title=Beyond the Pandemic: Leading Practices for the Future of Telemedicine |date= |publisher= |access-date=}}</ref> Examples cited in media coverage include [[DoktorABC]]<ref>{{cite news |date= |title=DoktorABC bringt die digitale Gesundheitsversorgung in Deutschland voran |url=https://www.laingbuissonnews.com/healthcare-markets-content/news-healthcare-markets-content/zava-enters-telemedicine-partnership-with-asda/ |access-date= |publisher= |language=de|work=LaingBuisson NewsLaingBuisson News}}</ref> and [[ZAVA]].<ref>{{cite news |date= |title=Zava enters telemedicine partnership with Asda |url=https://www.focus.de/kaufberatung/doktorabc-bringt-die-digitale-gesundheitsversorgung-in-deutschland-voran_5928fd0c-644e-452e-8565-403165004d61.html |publisher=|work=Focus Online}}</ref>The Clinical Telemedicine and Online Counselling service of the University Hospital of Zurich is currently being revised and will be offered in a new form in the future.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.usz.ch/Seiten/Telemedizin.aspx|title=Willkommen am UniversitätsSpital Zürich|website=www.usz.ch|language=de-CH|access-date=2020-01-23|archive-date=2020-01-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200117122940/http://www.usz.ch/Seiten/Telemedizin.aspx}}</ref>

== Developing countries ==
For developing countries, telemedicine and [[eHealth]] can be the only means of healthcare provision in remote areas. For example, the difficult financial situation in many African states and lack of trained health professionals has meant that the majority of the people in sub-Saharan Africa are badly disadvantaged in medical care, and in remote areas with low population density, direct healthcare provision is often very poor<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20160205083116/http://euroafrica-ict.org.sigma-orionis.com/downloads/Coop_Forum/SessionC/Adesina_Iluyemi.pdf ''Refocusing Europe-Africa Strategy: Strategic Importance of eHealth''] NEPAD. Accessed 28 January 2016.</ref> However, provision of telemedicine and eHealth from urban centers or from other countries is hampered by the lack of communications infrastructure, with no landline phone or broadband internet connection, little or no mobile connectivity, and often not even a reliable electricity supply.<ref>Gerhard Bethscheider [http://www.worldteleport.org/news/249029/Satellite-Is-Vital-For-A-Unified-Global-e-Health-System...-An-SES-Techcom-Services-Perspective-.htm ''Satellite is vital for a unified, global, E-Health system''] September 2015 World Teleport Association. Accessed 28 January 2016.</ref>

=== Telemedicine in developing countries ===

India has broad rural-urban population and rural India is bereaved from medical facilities, giving telemedicine a space for growth in India. Deprived education and medical professionals in rural areas is the reason behind government's ideology to use technology to bridge this gap. Remote areas not only present a number of challenges for the service providers but also for the families who are accessing these services. Since 2018, telemedicine has expanded in India. It has undertaken a new way for doctor consultations. On 25 March 2020, in the wake of COVID-19 pandemic, the [[Ministry of Health and Family Welfare]] issued India's Telemedicine Practice Guidelines.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Telemedicine Practice Guidelines of India |url=https://www.reclica.com/telemedicine-guidelines.html}}</ref> The Board of Governors entasked by the Health Ministry published an amendment to the [[Indian Medical Council]] (Professional Conduct, Etiquette and Ethics) Regulations, 2002 that gave much-needed statutory support for the practice of telemedicine in India. == History ==
The development and history of telehealth or telemedicine (terms used interchangeably in literature) is deeply rooted in the history and development in not only technology but also society itself. Humans have long sought to relay important messages through [[torch]]es, [[Semaphore line|optical telegraphy]], [[electroscope]]s, and [[Wireless|wireless transmission]]. Early forms of telemedicine achieved with telephone and radio have been supplemented with [[videotelephony]], advanced [[Medical diagnosis|diagnostic methods]] supported by [[Client–server model|distributed client/server applications]], and additionally with telemedical devices to support in-home care.<ref name="Sachpazidis"/>  Telehealth was originally developed to provide healthcare access for patients in rural and underserved communities where medical specialists were not readily available.

In the 21st century, with the advent of the [[internet]], [[Mobile device|portable devices]] and other such digital devices are taking a transformative role in healthcare and its delivery.<ref name="Bashshur-2009">{{cite book |last1=Bashshur |first1=Rashid |last2=Shannon |first2=Gary William |title=History of Telemedicine: Evolution, Context, and Transformation |date=2009 |publisher=Mary Ann Liebert |isbn=978-1-934854-11-2 }}{{pn|date=July 2025}}</ref>

=== Earliest instances ===
Although, [[traditional medicine]] relies on in-person care, the need and want for remote care has existed from the Roman and pre-Hippocratic periods in antiquity. The elderly and infirm who could not visit temples for medical care sent representatives to convey information on symptoms and bring home a diagnosis as well as treatment.<ref name="Bashshur-2009" /> In Africa, villagers would use [[smoke signal]]s to warn neighboring villages of disease outbreak.<ref name="Nakajima-2006">{{cite book |doi=10.1109/HEALTH.2006.246471 |chapter=The Asia Pacific telecommunity's telemedicine activities |title=HEALTHCOM 2006 8th International Conference on e-Health Networking, Applications and Services |date=2006 |last1=Nakajima |first1=I. |last2=Sastrokusumo |first2=U. |last3=Mishra |first3=S.K. |last4=Komiya |first4=R. |last5=Malik |first5=A.Z. |last6=Tanuma |first6=T. |pages=280–282 |isbn=0-7803-9704-5 }}</ref> The beginnings of telehealth have existed through primitive forms of communication and technology.<ref name="Bashshur-2009" /> The exact date of origin for Telehealth is unknown, but it was known to have been used during the [[Bubonic plague|Bubonic Plague]]. That version of telehealth was far different from how we know it today. During that time, they were communicating by [[heliograph]] and bonfire. Those were used to notify other groups of people about famine and war.<ref name="Cuffia 84–85">{{Cite journal| vauthors = Cuffia A |date=2019-01-02|title=The Medical Library Association Guide to Developing Consumer Health Collections |journal= Journal of Hospital Librarianship |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=84–85 |doi=10.1080/15323269.2019.1568127 }}</ref> Those are not using any form of technology yet but are starting to spread the idea of connectivity among groups of people who geographically could not be together.

=== 1800s to early 1900s ===
As technology developed and wired communication became increasingly commonplace, the ideas surrounding telehealth began emerging. The earliest telehealth encounter can be traced to [[Alexander Graham Bell]] in 1876, when he used his early telephone as a means of getting help from his assistant Mr. Watson after he spilt acid on his trousers. Another instance of early telehealth, specifically telemedicine was reported in ''[[The Lancet]]'' in 1879. An anonymous writer described a case where a doctor successfully diagnosed a child over the telephone in the middle of the night.<ref name="Bashshur-2009" /> This Lancet issue, also further discussed the potential of Remote Patient Care in order to avoid unnecessary house visits, which were part of routine health care during the 1800s.<ref name="Bashshur-2009" /><ref name="Zundel-1996">{{cite journal | vauthors = Zundel KM | title = Telemedicine: history, applications, and impact on librarianship | journal = Bulletin of the Medical Library Association | volume = 84 | issue = 1 | pages = 71–9 | date = January 1996 | pmid = 8938332 | pmc = 226126 }}</ref> Other instances of telehealth during this period came from the [[American Civil War]], during which telegraphs were used to deliver casualty/mortality lists, medical care to soldiers,<ref name="Zundel-1996" /> and ordering further medical supplies.<ref name= Bonica2024>{{cite journal |last1=Bonica |first1=Gina M. |last2=Johns |first2=Richard W. |last3=Jadvar |first3=Hossein |title=Telehealth and Telemedicine: Regulatory and Medicolegal Landscape |journal=Clinical Nuclear Medicine |date=July 2024 |volume=49 |issue=7 |pages=644–647 |doi=10.1097/RLU.0000000000005254 |pmid=38769654 }}</ref>

As the 1900s started, physicians quickly found a use for the telephone making it a prime communication channel to contact patients and other physicians.<ref name="Cuffia 84–85"/> Over the next fifty-plus years, the telephone was a staple for medical communication. As the 1930s came around, radio communication played a key role, especially during World War I. It was specifically used to communicate with remote areas such as Alaska and Australia.<ref name="Cuffia 84–85"/> They used the radio to communicate medical information. During the Vietnam War, radio communication had become more advanced and was now used to send medical teams in helicopters to help. This then brought together the Aerial Medical Service (AMS) who used telegraphs, radios, and planes to help care for people who lived in remote areas.

From the late 1800s to the early 1900s the early foundations of [[Wireless|wireless communication]] were laid down.<ref name="Bashshur-2009" /> [[Radio]]s provided an easier and near instantaneous form of communication. The use of radio to deliver healthcare became accepted for remote areas.<ref name="Bashshur-2009" /><ref name="Maheu-2002">{{cite book |last1=Maheu |first1=Marlene |last2=Whitten |first2=Pamela |last3=Allen |first3=Ace |title=E-Health, Telehealth, and Telemedicine: A Guide to Startup and Success |date=2002 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-0-7879-5903-6 }}{{pn|date=July 2025}}</ref> The [[Royal Flying Doctor Service]] in Australia is an example of the early adoption of radios in telehealth.<ref name="Nakajima-2006" />

In 1925 the inventor [[Hugo Gernsback]] wrote an article for the magazine ''[[Science and Invention]]'' which included a prediction of a future where patients could be treated remotely by doctors through a device he called a "teledactyl". His descriptions of the device are similar to what would later become possible with new technology.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Novak M | date = 14 March 2012 | url = https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/telemedicine-predicted-in-1925-124140942/ | title = Telemedicine Predicted in 1925 | work = The Smithsonian Institution }}</ref>

=== Mid-1900s to 1980s ===
When the American [[NASA|National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)]] began plans to send astronauts into space, the need for telemedicine became clear. In order to monitor their astronauts in space, telemedicine capabilities were built into the [[spacecraft]] as well as the first [[Space suit|spacesuits]].<ref name="Bashshur-2009" /><ref name="Maheu-2002" /> Additionally, during this period, telehealth and telemedicine were promoted in different countries especially the United States and Canada.<ref name="Bashshur-2009" /> [[Carrier Sekani Family Services]] helped pioneer telehealth in British Columbia and Canada, according to its CEO Warner Adam.<ref>

Technological advancements occurred when NASA sent men to space. Engineers for NASA created biomedical telemetry and [[telecommunications]] systems.<ref name="Cuffia 84–85"/> NASA technology monitored vitals such as blood pressure, heart rate, respiration rate, and temperature. After the technology was created, it then became the base of telehealth medicine for the public.

[[Massachusetts General Hospital]] and Boston's [[Logan International Airport]] had a role in the early use of telemedicine, which more or less coincided with NASA's foray into telemedicine through the use of physiologic monitors for astronauts.<ref>[http://tie.telemed.org/articles/article.asp?path=articles&article=tmhistory_nb_tie95.xml "A Brief History of Telemedicine" ] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071124075453/http://tie.telemed.org/articles/article.asp?path=articles&article=tmhistory_nb_tie95.xml|date=2007-11-24}}, Telemedicine Information Exchange website, (Accessed December 10, 2008)</ref> On October 26, 1960, a plane struck a flock of birds upon takeoff, killing many passengers and leaving a number wounded. Due to the extreme complexity of trying to get all the medical personnel out from the hospital, the practical solution became telehealth.<ref name = "Weinstein_2011">{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-56917-4_1 |chapter=First Trainees: The Golden Anniversary of the Early History of Telemedicine Education at the Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard (1968–1970) |title=Telemedicine, Telehealth and Telepresence |date=2021 |last1=Weinstein |first1=Ronald S. |last2=Holcomb |first2=Michael J. |last3=Krupinski |first3=Elizabeth A. |last4=Latifi |first4=Rifat |pages=3–18 |isbn=978-3-030-56916-7 }}</ref> This was expanded upon in 1967, when Dr. [[Kenneth_T._Bird]] at Massachusetts General founded one of the first telemedicine clinics. The clinic addressed the fundamental problem of delivering occupational and emergency health services to employees and travellers at the airport, located three congested miles from the hospital. Clinicians at the hospital would provide consultation services to patients who were at the airport. Consultations were achieved through microwave audio as well as video links.<ref name="Bashshur-2009" /><ref name="Allan-2006" /> The airport began seeing over a hundred patients a day at its nurse-run clinic that cared for victims of plane crashes and other accidents, taking vital signs, electrocardiograms, and video images that were sent to Massachusetts General.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Buhler |first1=Leo H. |title=Recollections of Pioneers in Xenotransplantation Research Edited by David K. C.Cooper, Nova Medicine and Health, Nova Science Publishers, New York, NY, 2018. |journal=Xenotransplantation |date=January 2019 |volume=26 |issue=1 |article-number=e12495 |doi=10.1111/xen.12495 }}</ref> Over 1,000 patients are documented as having received remote treatment from doctors at MGH using the clinic's two-way audiovisual microwave circuit.<ref>[http://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/457684 "Highlights from the Eighth Annual Meeting of the American Telemedicine Association"] (Accessed December 10, 2008), Medscape website</ref> One notable story featured a woman who got off a flight in Boston and was experiencing chest pain. They performed a workup at the airport, took her to the telehealth suite where Raymond Murphy appeared on the television, and had a conversation with her. While this was happening, another doctor took notes and the nurses took vitals and any test that Murphy ordered.<ref name = "Weinstein_2011" /> At this point, telehealth was becoming more mainstream and was starting to become more technologically advanced, which created a viable option for patients.

In 1964, the Nebraska Psychiatric Institute began using television links to form two-way communication with the Norfolk State Hospital which was 112 miles away for the education and consultation purposes between clinicians in the two locations.<ref name="Allan-2006">{{Cite web|url=http://electronicdesign.com/components/brief-history-telemedicine|title=A Brief History Of Telemedicine| vauthors = Allan R |date=28 June 2006|publisher=Electronic Design}}</ref>

In 1972 the [[United States Department of Health, Education, and Welfare|Department of Health, Education and Welfare]] in the United States approved funding for seven telemedicine projects across different states. This funding was renewed and two further projects were funded the following year.<ref name="Bashshur-2009" /><ref name="Allan-2006" />

In March 1972, the San Bernardino County Medical Society officially implemented its Tel-Med program, a system of prerecorded health-related messages, with a log of 50 tapes.<ref | pmid = 516712 | pmc = 1271730 }}</ref><ref name="Rovner-1979">{{Cite news | vauthors = Rovner S |date=7 September 1979 |title=Health Talk: With Tel-Med, Medical Information Is Only a Phone Call Away |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1979/09/07/health-talk-with-tel-med-medical-information-is-only-a-phone-call-away/5cf7ba20-a2da-454a-a9c8-868ac832e52a/ |access-date=12 May 2022}}</ref> The nonprofit initiative began in 1971 as a local medical project to ease the doctor shortage in the expanding [[San Bernardino Valley]] and improve the public's access to sound medical information.<ref name="Rovner-1979" /><ref name="Harer-1979" /> It covered subjects ranging from [[Cannabis (drug)|cannabis]] to [[vaginitis]].<ref name="Harer-1979" /> In January 1973, in response to state.<ref>{{Cite news |date=10 January 1973 |title=Tel-Med Proves Its Versatility |page=22 |work=The San Bernardino Sun |url=https://cdnc.ucr.edu/?a=d&d=SBS19730110.1.22&srpos=209&e=------197-en--20--201--txt-txIN--------1 |access-date=12 May 2022}}</ref> That spring, programs were implemented in [[San Diego]] and available in Spanish as well as English, and serviced over 65 million people in 180 cities around the country.<ref name="Harer-1979" />

=== 1980s to 1990s – maturation and renaissance ===
Telehealth projects underway before and during the 1980s would take off but fail to enter mainstream healthcare.<ref name="Nakajima-2006" /><ref name="Maheu-2002" /> As a result, this period of telehealth history is called the "maturation" stage and made way for sustainable growth.<ref name="Bashshur-2009" /> Although state funding in North America was beginning to run low, different hospitals began to launch their own telehealth initiatives.<ref name="Bashshur-2009" /> NASA provided an ATS-3 satellite to enable medical care communications of [[American Red Cross]] and [[Pan American Health Organization]] response teams, following the [[1985 Mexico City earthquake]]. The agency then launched its SateLife/HealthNet programme to increase health service connectivity in developing countries. In 1997, NASA sponsored [[Yale]]'s Medical Informatics and Technology Applications Consortium project.<ref name="Maheu-2002" /><ref>{{cite news | url = https://www.forbes.com/sites/jonmarkman/2018/08/26/nasa-incubated-healthcare-provider-is-out-of-this-world/#7b5ff82b62ac | title = NASA-Incubated Healthcare Provider Is Out Of This World | vauthors = Markman J | date = August 26, 2018 | access-date=2019-10-06}}</ref>

Florida first experimented with "primitive" telehealth in its [[Florida Department of Corrections|prisons]] during the latter 1980s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Berger |first1=Eric |title=Telemedicine: Has Its Time Come? |journal=Annals of Emergency Medicine |date=November 2010 |volume=56 |issue=5 |pages=A15–A17 |doi=10.1016/j.annemergmed.2010.09.008 |pmid=21064235 }}</ref> Working with Doctors Oscar W. Boultinghouse and Michael J. Davis, from the early 1990s to 2007; Glenn G. Hammack led the [[University of Texas Medical Branch]] (UTMB) development of a pioneering telehealth program in [[Texas Department of Criminal Justice|Texas state prisons]]. The three UTMB alumni would, in 2007, co-found telehealth provider NuPhysician.<ref>{{cite news | url = https://www.nytimes.com/2010/05/30/business/30telemed.html | title = The Doctor Will See You Now. Please Log On. | vauthors = Freudenheim M | newspaper = The New York Times | date = May 29, 2010 | access-date = 2019-10-03}}</ref>

The first interactive telemedicine system, operating over standard telephone lines, designed to [[Remote diagnostics|remotely diagnose]] and treat patients requiring cardiac resuscitation ([[defibrillation]]) was developed and launched by an American company, MedPhone Corporation, in 1989. A year later under the leadership of its President/CEO S Eric Wachtel, MedPhone introduced a mobile cellular version, the MDPhone. Twelve hospitals in the U.S. served as receiving and treatment centers.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Blyth WJ | title = Telecommunications, Concepts, Development, and Management | edition = Second | publisher = Glencoe/McCgraw-Hill | year = 1990 | pages = 280–282 |isbn=978-0-02-680841-5}}</ref>

=== At-home virtual care ===
As the expansion of telehealth continued in 1990 Maritime Health Services (MHS) was a big part of the initiation for occupational health services. They sent a medical officer aboard the Pacific trawler that allowed for round-the-clock communication with a physician. The system that allows for this is called the Medical Consultation Network (MedNet). MedNet is a video chatting system that has live audio and visual so the physician on the other end of the call can see and hear what is happening. MetNet can be used from anywhere, not just aboard ships.<ref name="Cuffia 84–85"/> Being able to provide onsite visual information allows remote patients expert emergency help and medical attention that saves money as well as lives. This has created a demand for at-home monitoring. At-home care has also become a large part of telehealth. Doctors or nurses will now give pre-op and post-op phone calls to check-in. There are also companies such as [[Lifeline Systems, Inc.|Lifeline]], which give the elderly a button to press in case of an emergency. That button will automatically call for emergency help. If someone has surgery and then is sent home, telehealth allows physicians to see how the patient is progressing without them having to stay in the hospital. TeleDiagnostic Systems of San Francisco is a company that has created a device that monitors sleep patterns, so people with sleep disorders do not have to stay the night at the hospital.<ref name="Cuffia 84–85"/> Another at-home device that was created was the Wanderer, which was attached to Alzheimer's patients or people who had dementia. It was attached to them so when they wandered off it notified the staff to allow them to go after them. All these devices allowed healthcare beyond hospitals to improve, which means that more people are being helped efficiently.

=== 2000s to present ===
The advent of high-speed [[Internet]], and the increasing adoption of [[Information and communications technology|ICT]] in traditional methods of care, spurred advances in telehealth delivery.<ref name="The Center for Connected Health Policy">{{Cite web|url=http://cchpca.org/what-is-telehealth|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120115222043/http://cchpca.org/what-is-telehealth|url-status=live|archive-date=January 15, 2012|title=What is Telehealth?|publisher=The Center for Connected Health Policy}}</ref> Increased access to portable devices, like laptops and mobile phones, made telehealth more plausible; the industry then expanded into health promotion, prevention and education.<ref name="Office for the Advancement of Telehealth-2022" /><ref name="CFP"/><ref name="Maheu-2002" />

In 2002, G. Byron Brooks, a former NASA surgeon and engineer who had also helped manage the [[University of Texas Medical Branch|UTMB]] Telemedicine program, co-founded [[Teladoc]] in [[Dallas, Texas]], which was then launched in 2005 as the first national telehealth provider.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.dmagazine.com/publications/d-ceo/2016/november/how-the-north-texas-telemedicine-revolution-began/ |title = How the North Texas Telemedicine Revolution Began | vauthors = Goodman M | newspaper = D Magazine | date = November 2016 | access-date = 2019-10-03}}</ref>

In the 2010s, integration of smart home telehealth technologies, such as health and wellness devices, software, and integrated [[Internet of things|IoT]], has accelerated the industry. Healthcare organizations are increasingly adopting the use of self-tracking and cloud-based technologies, and innovative data analytic approaches to accelerate telehealth delivery.{{citation needed|date=October 2019}}<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Morita |first1=Plinio P |last2=Sahu |first2=Kirti Sundar |last3=Oetomo |first3=Arlene |date=2022-02-16 |title=Health Monitoring Using Smart Home Technologies: Scoping Review (Preprint) |doi=10.2196/preprints.37347 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Dinesen B, Nonnecke B, Lindeman D, Toft E, Kidholm K, Jethwani K, Young HM, Spindler H, Oestergaard CU, Southard JA, Gutierrez M, Anderson N, Albert NM, Han JJ, Nesbitt T | title = Personalized Telehealth in the Future: A Global Research Agenda | journal = Journal of Medical Internet Research | volume = 18 | issue = 3 | pages = e53 | date = March 2016 | pmid = 26932229 | pmc = 4795318 | doi = 10.2196/jmir.5257 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

In 2015, [[Mercy (healthcare organization)|Mercy Health system]] opened [[Mercy Virtual]], in Chesterfield, Missouri, the world's first medical facility dedicated solely to telemedicine.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Allen |first1=Arthur |title=A hospital without patients |url=https://www.politico.com/agenda/story/2017/11/08/virtual-hospital-mercy-st-louis-000573/ |work=The Agenda |publisher=Politico |date=8 November 2017 }}</ref>

==== COVID-19 ====
{{See also|#Health care quality and barriers to adoption}}
Telehealth expanded significantly during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], becoming a vital means of medical communication. It allows doctors to return to humanizing the patient.<ref name="Schiffman">{{cite news |last1=Schiffman |first1=Richard |date=25 February 2021 |title=Learning to Listen to Patients' Stories |newspaper=The New York Times |id={{ProQuest|2492893443}} |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/02/25/well/live/narrative-medicine.html }}</ref> It forces them to listen to what people have to say and from there make a diagnosis. Studies have demonstrated high trust in telehealth expressed by patients during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Costantino A, Noviello D, Mazza S, Berté R, Caprioli F, Vecchi M |title=Trust in telemedicine from IBD outpatients during the COVID-19 pandemic |journal=Dig Liver Dis |volume=53 |issue=3 |pages=291–4 |date=March 2021 |pmid=33187917 |pmc=7644233 |doi=10.1016/j.dld.2020.10.035 }}</ref> Among patients with [[Inflammatory bowel disease]] 4 out of 5 considered telemedicine as valuable tool for their management, and 85%) wanted to have a telemedicine service at their center. However, only 1 out of 4 believed that it may guarantee the same level of care as the in-person visit.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bossa |first1=F. |last2=Valvano |first2=M.R. |last3=Vetrone |first3=L.M. |last4=Guerra |first4=M. |last5=Lopetuso |first5=L.R. |last6=Carparelli |first6=S. |last7=Mignini |first7=I. |last8=Cocomazzi |first8=F. |last9=Napolitano |first9=D. |last10=Costantino |first10=A. |last11=Caprioli |first11=F. |last12=Gasbarrini |first12=A. |last13=Perri |first13=F. |last14=Papa |first14=A. |title=Evaluation of factors associated with trust in telemedicine in patients with inflammatory bowel disease during COVID-19 pandemic: a multicenter cross-sectional survey |journal=European Review for Medical and Pharmacological Sciences |date=October 2022 |volume=26 |issue=19 |pages=7277–7284 |doi=10.26355/eurrev_202210_29921 |pmid=36263539 }}</ref> Some researchers claim this creates an environment that encourages greater vulnerability among patients in self disclosure in the practice of narrative medicine.<ref name="Schiffman"/> Telehealth allows for Zoom calls and video chats from across the world checking in on patients and speaking to physicians. Universities are now ensuring that medical students graduate with proficient telehealth communication skills.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Thomas EE, Haydon HM, Mehrotra A, Caffery LJ, Snoswell CL, Banbury A, Smith AC | title = Building on the momentum: Sustaining telehealth beyond COVID-19 | journal = Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare | volume = 28 | issue = 4 | pages = 301–8 | date = May 2022 | pmid = 32985380 | doi = 10.1177/1357633X20960638 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Experts suggest that telehealth has become a vital part of medical care; with more virtual options becoming available. The pandemic era also identified the "potential to significantly improve global health equity" through telehealth and other virtual care technologies.<ref>{{Cite web | url = https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2023/01/telemedicine-global-health-equity-at-home-davos23/ | title = Telemedicine could help the world achieve health equity by bringing care to the home - here's how | publisher = [[World Economic Forum]] | date = 12 January 2023 | access-date=2023-01-12}}</ref>

== Telehealth versus in-person on treatment and follow-up visits study ==
A retrospective study in 2023 examining 1,589,014 adult primary care patients within an integrated healthcare system in the U.S. found that patients who initially had a telehealth visit were less likely to receive prescriptions, lab tests, or imaging compared to those who had an in-office visit. However, these same telehealth patients had higher rates of in-person follow-up visits. The study revealed that, out of the 2,357,598 primary care visits, 49.2% were in-office, 31.3% were telephone visits, and 19.5% were video visits. Office visits led to higher rates of prescriptions (46.8%), lab tests (41.4%), and imaging (20.5%) compared to video (38.4%, 27.4%, and 11.9%, respectively) and telephone visits (34.6%, 22.8%, and 8.7%, respectively). In contrast, patients who had telephone or video visits were more likely to have in-person follow-up visits, with 7.6% of telephone, 6.2% of video, and only 1.3% of office visit patients returning for primary care follow-up. Furthermore, rates of emergency department visits and hospitalizations were higher for those who had telemedicine visits, though these differences were minimal. The study's limitations include the inability to generalize findings to healthcare settings without telemedicine services or to patients without insurance or a primary care provider. The reasons for increased in-person healthcare utilization were also not captured, and long-term follow-up was not conducted.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Reed |first1=Mary |last2=Huang |first2=Jie |last3=Somers |first3=Madeline |last4=Hsueh |first4=Loretta |last5=Graetz |first5=Ilana |last6=Millman |first6=Andrea |last7=Muelly |first7=Emilie |last8=Gopalan |first8=Anjali |title=Telemedicine Versus In-Person Primary Care: Treatment and Follow-up Visits |journal=Annals of Internal Medicine |date=October 2023 |volume=176 |issue=10 |pages=1349–1357 |doi=10.7326/m23-1335 |pmid=37844311 |pmc=11382601 }}</ref>
